--- Slide 1 ---
Haemoglobin Disorders I Department of Haematology & Blood Transfusion, College of Medicine, UNILAG Professor Titi Adeyemo
--- Slide 2 ---
Learning Objectives At the end of the lectures, the student should be able to: Describe what is haemoglobinopathy (Haemoglobin disorder) Describe the geographical distribution of haemoglobinopathies Describe the molecular basis of the haemoglobinopathies. Describe the inheritance pattern of haemoglobin disorders. Describe the pathophysiology of the haemoglobinopathies. Describe the general haematological and clinical features of Haemoglobinopathies. Describe the diagnosis & management of common haemoglobin disorders. Discuss the prevention programs for haemoglobinopathies
--- Slide 3 ---
Lectures Haemoglobin Disorders I: Define Haemoglobinopathies & Describe the Thalassemia Haemoglobin Disorders II: Sickle cell Disease: Pathophysiology, Clinical and Laboratory Features & Management Haemoglobin Disorders III: Other abnormal structural variants
--- Slide 4 ---
What are the haemoglobinopathies? The haemoglobinopathies are a group of disorders passed down through families (inherited) in which there is abnormal production or structure of the haemoglobin molecule. Haemoglobinopathies are caused by mutations in globin genes, which encode for the globin proteins of haemoglobin, causing decreased or defective production of haemoglobin, haemolysis, and anaemia. Haemoglobinopathies are the commonest monogenic diseases because almost 7% of the worldwide population are carriers. They have originally emerged from the Mediterranean regions, large parts of Asia and Africa. However, the slave trade and international migration contributed to their spread from those areas to all over the world.
--- Slide 5 ---
Classification of Haemoglobin Disorders Haemoglobin disorders are be broadly classified into two general categories Qualitative disorders of globin structure: structural variants of haemoglobin Quantitative disorders of globin chain synthesis/accumulation
--- Slide 6 ---
Can be BOTH!
--- Slide 8 ---
Geographic distribution of the haemoglobinopathies Commonest genetic defect worldwide with an estimated 269 million carriers. Inherited haemoglobin disorders were originally characteristic of the tropics and subtropics but are now common worldwide due to migration. In populations in which malaria is (or was) endemic, 3 to 40% of individuals carry one of these significant variants. Haemoglobin disorders are distributed across South-east Asia in a line stretching from Southern China down the Malaysian Peninsula to Indonesian islands.
--- Slide 10 ---
Hb AS is very widespread and is found in up to one in four West Africans, (25%). It is maintained at this level because of the protection against malaria that it offers. Also distributed across the Mediterranean, Middle East, and Indian Subcontinent. The distribution of the defect is thought to be due to partial protection for carriers from plasmodium falciparum malaria. β thalassaemia syndrome is found in the Mediterranean region especially Greece, Italy, some part of Spain While α-thalassaemia is more common in the Far East/ South-east Asia.
--- Slide 12 ---
The world distribution of haemoglobinopathies overlaps the geographic distribution of malaria. The prevalence has increased in previously non-endemic areas owing to historical and recent immigration flows, slave-trade, trading activities and colonization. In all these regions there is a high prevalence of α thalassaemia. It is believed that carriers of α thalassaemia are protected against malaria and that natural selection is responsible for elevating and maintaining their gene frequencies.
--- Slide 13 ---
The most common inherited Hb disorder: α plus (α + ) thalassaemia, is usually harmless. However, people who inherit combinations of haemoglobins S, C, E, D Punjab, β thalassaemia, or α zero (α 0 ) thalassaemia may have a serious haemoglobin disorder. Homozygous sickle cell anaemia (Hb SS) is the most common while the doubly heterozygote conditions of Hb SC and Hb Sβ thal also cause sickling disease. Haemoglobin C defect is most frequent in West Africa. The highest frequency is found in Burkina fasso & Ghana followed by western part of Nigeria. This is due to the fact that these areas were or are still afflicted with malaria and Hb C confers a relative protection against malaria.
--- Slide 14 ---
Types of genetic defects causing Haemoglobinopathies Deletion of a globin gene Partial deletion of a globin gene Fusion of genes Production of non-functional mRNA Abnormal gene transcription Point mutations resulting in dysfunction of the genes Mutations affecting termination of translation giving rise to elongated but unstable globin chain. The most common genetic disorder of haemoglobin is those caused by point mutation followed by deletion.

Thalassaemia Reduced production of β chains β thalassaemia Reduced production of α chains α thalassaemia Other variant: δ thalassaemia, δβ -thalassaemia style.visibility ppt_x ppt_y style.visibility ppt_x ppt_y style.visibility ppt_x ppt_y style.visibility ppt_x ppt_y style.visibility ppt_x ppt_y

Inheritance of β thalassaemia β- thalassemias are caused by point mutations or, more rarely, deletions in the β globin gene on chromosome 11, leading to reduced ( β +) or absent ( β 0) synthesis of the β chains of hemoglobin (Hb). Transmission is autosomal recessive; however, dominant mutations have also been reported. Effect on β chain production variable

What are the haemoglobinopathies? The haemoglobinopathies are a group of disorders passed down through families (inherited) in which there is abnormal production or structure of the haemoglobin molecule. Haemoglobinopathies are caused by mutations in globin genes, which encode for the globin proteins of haemoglobin, causing decreased or defective production of haemoglobin, haemolysis, and anaemia. Haemoglobinopathies are the commonest monogenic diseases because almost 7% of the worldwide population are carriers. They have originally emerged from the Mediterranean regions, large parts of Asia and Africa. However, the slave trade and international migration contributed to their spread from those areas to all over the world.

Classification of Haemoglobin Disorders Haemoglobin disorders are be broadly classified into two general categories Qualitative disorders of globin structure: structural variants of haemoglobin Quantitative disorders of globin chain synthesis/accumulation
Can be BOTH!

Geographic distribution of the haemoglobinopathies Commonest genetic defect worldwide with an estimated 269 million carriers. Inherited haemoglobin disorders were originally characteristic of the tropics and subtropics but are now common worldwide due to migration. In populations in which malaria is (or was) endemic, 3 to 40% of individuals carry one of these significant variants. Haemoglobin disorders are distributed across South-east Asia in a line stretching from Southern China down the Malaysian Peninsula to Indonesian islands.

Hb AS is very widespread and is found in up to one in four West Africans, (25%). It is maintained at this level because of the protection against malaria that it offers. Also distributed across the Mediterranean, Middle East, and Indian Subcontinent. The distribution of the defect is thought to be due to partial protection for carriers from plasmodium falciparum malaria. β thalassaemia syndrome is found in the Mediterranean region especially Greece, Italy, some part of Spain While α-thalassaemia is more common in the Far East/ South-east Asia.

The world distribution of haemoglobinopathies overlaps the geographic distribution of malaria. The prevalence has increased in previously non-endemic areas owing to historical and recent immigration flows, slave-trade, trading activities and colonization. In all these regions there is a high prevalence of α thalassaemia. It is believed that carriers of α thalassaemia are protected against malaria and that natural selection is responsible for elevating and maintaining their gene frequencies.

The most common inherited Hb disorder: α plus (α + ) thalassaemia, is usually harmless. However, people who inherit combinations of haemoglobins S, C, E, D Punjab, β thalassaemia, or α zero (α 0 ) thalassaemia may have a serious haemoglobin disorder. Homozygous sickle cell anaemia (Hb SS) is the most common while the doubly heterozygote conditions of Hb SC and Hb Sβ thal also cause sickling disease. Haemoglobin C defect is most frequent in West Africa. The highest frequency is found in Burkina fasso & Ghana followed by western part of Nigeria. This is due to the fact that these areas were or are still afflicted with malaria and Hb C confers a relative protection against malaria.

The most common genetic disorder of haemoglobin is those caused by point mutation followed by deletion.

--- Slide 1 ---
Haemoglobin Disorders II: Sickle Cell disease Department of Haematology & Blood Transfusion, College of Medicine, UNILAG Prof. Titi Adeyemo
--- Slide 2 ---
Common types of abnormal Hb HbS (α 2 β 2 6 ), Gln Val 6th position on the β HbC (α 2 β 2 6 ), Gln Lys 6th position on the β HbD (Punjab) ( α 2 ß 2 121 ) , Glu Gl n 121 ST position on the β HbD (Ibadan) (α 2 ß 2 87 ), Threonine lys 87th position on the β HbE ( α 2 ß 2 26 ) Gly lys 26th position on the β Rare Hb O-Arab ( α 2 β 2 121 ) Glu → Lys (Hb O-Arab). Mutations of heterozygotes for Hb O-Arab have been reported in Saudi Arabia, North Africa, Sudan, the Mediterranean and the United States.
--- Slide 3 ---
Sickle Cell disease Sickle cell disease is a group of haemoglobin disorders in which the sickle β-globin gene is inherited. The sickle β-globin abnormality is caused by substitution of valine for glutamic acid in position 6 in the β globin-chain. Homozygous sickle cell anaemia ( HbSS ) is the most common while the doubly heterozygote conditions of HbSC and Hb Sβ thal also cause sickling disease. HbAS , the carrier status is very widespread and is found in up to one in four West Africans, (25%). It is maintained at this level because of the protection against malaria that it offers.
--- Slide 4 ---
Homozygous Disease: Hb SS; Sickle cell anaemia. T he inheritance of 2 HbS gene one each from both parent. The disease was first described in 1904 by a Chicago based physcian , Dr. James Herrick who reported "peculiar elongated and sickle shaped" red blood cells in a young man of negroid origin. The patient had come to Dr. Herrick with complaints of shortness of breath, heart palpitations, abdominal pain, and aches and pains in his muscles. He also felt tired all the time, had headaches, experienced attacks of dizziness, and had ulcers on his legs. After noting these symptoms, the doctor took samples of his blood
--- Slide 5 ---
Genetic basis of Sickle cell anaemia ( HbSS ) Single point mutation on the β gene at 17 th nucleotide, 6 th Codon, aa in position 6, resulting in valine instead of glutamine For comparison, Hb C a mutation at the same spot, leads to lysine instead of glutamine
--- Slide 6 ---
Haemoglobin S production arises from an altered (mutated) “S” gene. Differ from HbA by one amino acid substitution.
--- Slide 7 ---
Pathogenesis The substitution of a valine for a glutamine results in decreased solubility of deoxy- HbS compared to deoxy- HbA . When deoxygenated, HbS tetramers form polymers which associate into bundles that precipitate in the red cell
--- Slide 9 ---
Consequences of polymerization of haemoglobin Sickling of red cells Loss of red blood cell deformability Haemolysis of red blood cells Vaso-occlusion of small vessels End organ damage
--- Slide 10 ---
Pathophysiologic effects of sickled cells . Red cells carrying Hb S constantly switch from normal shape on the arterial side to sickled shape on the venous side. Eventually, some cells become irreversibly deformed, resulting in: 1. Extra-vascular haemolysis . Conscientious function of the spleen to remove damaged or deformed cells targets the cells that cannot traverse the narrow openings of the splenic sinusoids. The cells are trapped and removed by macrophages. The deformed cells compromise the blood supply of the spleen causing repeated small infarctions and eventual loss of splenic function. Replacement of cells carrying HbS with the same abnormal cells causes anaemia because of continuous early destruction of the cells by the spleen and, later, by the RES.
--- Slide 11 ---
2. Compromise of Microcirculation . As red cells carrying HbS become sickled and lose their ability to traverse narrow passages. They create a blockage that obstructs blood flow into the tissue. Impaired rheology of the blood and aggregation of sickle erythrocytes with neutrophils, platelets, and endothelial cells causes stasis of blood flow and is referred to as vaso -occlusion. The local anoxia that results from the blockage increase oxygen extraction from the trapped red cells and further aggravates the deoxygenation and polymerization of abnormal haemoglobin. The compensatory action of the adjacent vessels releases more oxygen from the cells. This increases sickling and causes exacerbation of the situation. Tissue damage from lack of oxygen is the cause of the acute and chronic pain characteristic of sickle cell crises . Vaso-occlusion promotes ischemia-reperfusion (I-R) injury
--- Slide 13 ---
Factors promoting sickling Temperature: exposure to extreme heat/cold. More of cold Dehydration Acidosis Hypoxemia: altitude, operations, obstetric delivery, stasis of the circulation, , violent exercise
--- Slide 14 ---
Factors opposing sickling The presence of non sickling haemoglobin: HbF HbA
--- Slide 15 ---
Inheritance
--- Slide 16 ---
If one parent has sickle-cell anaemia (SS) and the other has sickle-cell trait (AS), there is a 50% chance of a child's having sickle-cell disease (SS) and a 50% chance of a child's having sickle-cell trait (AS). When both parents have sickle-cell trait (AS), a child has a 25% chance (1 of 4) of sickle-cell anaemia (SS), as shown in the diagram.
--- Slide 17 ---
Clinical Features Clinical features are of severe haemolytic anaemia punctuated by crises. The symptoms of anaemia are often mild in relation to the severity of the anaemia because HbS gives up oxygen (O 2 ) to tissues relatively easily compared with HbA , its O 2 dissociation curve being shifted to the right. The clinical expression of Hb SS is very variable, some patients having an almost normal life, free of crises but others develop severe crises even as infants and may die in early childhood or as young adults .
--- Slide 18 ---
Sickle Cell Anemia: Clinical Features Consequences of Haemolysis Anaemia Jaundice Gallstones Vasculopathies: Peripheral blood smear with sickle cells Jaundice
--- Slide 19 ---
Crises may be:
--- Slide 20 ---
Vaso-occlusive (Pain) crises These are the most frequent and are precipitated by such factors as infection, acidosis, dehydration or de-oxygenation (e.g. altitude, operations, obstetric delivery, stasis of the circulation, exposure to cold, violent exercise). Infarcts can occur in a variety of organs including the bones (hips, shoulders and vertebrae are commonly affected), the lungs and the spleen. The most serious vaso -occlusion is of the brain (Ischemic stroke occurs in 7% of all patients) or spinal cord. Transcranial Doppler ultrasonography detects abnormal blood flow indicative of arterial stenosis. This predicts stroke in children. This can be largely prevented by regular blood transfusions in these cases.
--- Slide 21 ---
The ‘hand-foot’ syndrome (painful dactylitis caused by infarcts of the small bones) is frequently the first presentation of the disease and may lead to digits of varying lengths.
--- Slide 22 ---
PRIAPISM Priapism is the persistent, painful purposeless erection of the penis. It is relatively common in young males with sickle cell anemia. The onset may be in early childhood or adolescence. Recurrent or severe episodes can result in future impotence. Treatment is often not satisfactory.

The patient had come to Dr. Herrick with complaints of shortness of breath, heart palpitations, abdominal pain, and aches and pains in his muscles. The cells are trapped and removed by macrophages. The deformed cells compromise the blood supply of the spleen causing repeated small infarctions and eventual loss of splenic function. Replacement of cells carrying HbS with the same abnormal cells causes anaemia because of continuous early destruction of the cells by the spleen and, later, by the RES.

A linear strand of DNA has one end where the OH - group attached to the 5-carbon is free ( ie 5 primer end or up stream end) while the other end in which the OH-group attached to the 3-carbon is free (3-primer end or down stream end) the 5 1 end and the 3 1 end of each DNA strands are always complementarily paired.

By convention, the strand shown at the top is the coding or sense strand but the strand at the bottom actually serves as template Four bases are required to specify for 20 commonly occurring amino acids in proteins. Therefore the genetic code has to be in triplets ( codon )

Here each amino acid is specified by one or more sequences of codon but these sequences that specifies amino acid are interrupted by intervening sequence (introns) that do not code for aas sequence of the proteins.

Picture: Acute hypogranular/microgranular variant of promyelocytic leukaemia showing a range of nuclear forms; note the typical bilobed nucleus, with the two lobes joined by an isthmus.
--- Slide 10 ---
LABORATORY DIAGNOSIS OF LEUKAEMIA Bone marrow trephine biopsy is indicated whenever there is a ‘dry tap’ or the aspirate obtained is aparticulate or dilute A core biopsy is often necessary in hairy cell leukaemia, acute panmyelosis with myelofibrosis, acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia, pancytopenia or leucoerythroblastic picture Picture: bone marrow trephine biospy showing acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia FAB M7 subtype, blast cells (left) and increased reticulin deposition (right)
--- Slide 11 ---
Cytochemistry/cytochemical stains With advances in immunophenotyping and other techniques, the role of cytochemistry in haematological diagnosis has declined considerably FAB M1 AML can be distinguished from ALL by means of a Sudan black B or a stain Acute monoblastic/monocytic leukaemia can be distinguished from large-cell lymphoma by means of a non-specific esterase stain Distinction between FAB M3 variant and M5b AML can be made by strong reactions for Sudan black B, myeloperoxidase and chloroacetate esterase and the latter by a positive non-specific esterase reaction Picture: Myeloperoxidase reaction in AML FAB M1 showing Auer rods LABORATORY DIAGNOSIS OF LEUKAEMIA
--- Slide 12 ---
Immunophenotyping permits the simultaneous assessment of forward light scatter (indicative of cell size), sideways light scatter (indicative of granularity and cell complexity), and the expression of surface membrane antigens. Confirmation of diagnosis of ALL, AML, CLL, mixed lineage acute leukaemia, assessment of clonality etc using specific CD markers etc using specific CD markers LABORATORY DIAGNOSIS OF LEUKAEMIA
--- Slide 13 ---
Cytogenetic analysis refers to study of chromosomes by recognition of their morphology and their characteristic banding pattern Conventional karyotyping Florescence in situ hybridization (FISH) Picture: karyogram of Giemsa-stained chromosomes showing t(9;22)(q34;q11.2). The derivative chromosome 22 is the Philadelphia chromosome LABORATORY DIAGNOSIS OF LEUKAEMIA
--- Slide 14 ---
LABORATORY DIAGNOSIS OF LEUKAEMIA Florescence in situ hybridization (FISH): is both a cytogenetic and molecular genetic technique since the morphology of the chromosomes can be recognized to some extent, at least in metaphase cells, but the probes used are dependent on hybridization to specific DNA sequences Screening for BCR–ABL1 fusion, detection of t(8;21)(q22;q22), t(15;17)(q22;q12), inv(16)(p13.1q22) or MLL rearrangement (KMT2Ar) in AML Picture: An explanatory diagram (top), karyogram of Giemsa-stained chromosomes showing del(5)(q13q31) (bottom left), and FISH showing retention of signal for 5p15 and loss of signal for 5q31 (bottom right) in a patient with 5q– syndrome
--- Slide 15 ---
LABORATORY DIAGNOSIS OF LEUKAEMIA Molecular genetic analysis includes Southern blotting (now little used in routine diagnosis), the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to study genomic DNA and reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) to study RNA after its reverse transcription Detection of leukaemia-related and lymphoma-related chromosomal rearrangements by demonstration of gene juxtaposition or fusion to confirm a diagnosis, Detection of gene mutations relevant to diagnosis, for example KIT D816V in systemic mastocytosis or either JAK2 V617F or JAK2 exon 12 mutation in polycythaemia vera Picture: PCR gel showing the various BCR–ABL1 transcripts that can be identified by PCR.
--- Slide 16 ---
LABORATORY DIAGNOSIS OF LEUKAEMIA Other methods Microarray analysis of gene expression Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS)
--- Slide 17 ---
TREATMENT OF LEUKAEMIA Treatment of leukaemia has improved significantly in recent years due to better supportive care and and improvement in specific management of the different entities. An assessment of the performance status of the patient also allows treatment to be individualised eg ECOG score, assessment of co-morbidity
--- Slide 18 ---
GENERAL SUPPORTIVE CARE FOR LEUKAEMIA Insertion of central venous catheter Blood product support eg packed red cells, apheresis platelets, irradiation Treatment of tumour lysis eg Allopurinol, Rasburicase Anti-emetic therapy Haemostatic support eg Vitamin K, Tranexamic acid, FFP Psychological support Reproductive issues eg sperm and oocyte banking Infection prophylaxis and treatment Pain management
--- Slide 19 ---
SPECIFIC TREAMTENT The definitive treatment of leukaemia is disease entity specific Innovation and drug discovery have revolutionized the treatment of leukaemia Different classes of drug are now available for the treatment of leukaemia These therapies are used solely or in combination in the different phases of treatment including induction, consolidation/delayed intensification, maintenance phases
--- Slide 20 ---
DRUGS USED IN THE TREATMENT OF LEUKAEMIA Cytotoxic drugs: Alkylating agents: cyclophosphamide, bendamustine Antimetabolites: methotrexate, mercaptopurine Cytotoxic antibiotics: daunorubicin Vinca alkaloids: vincristine
--- Slide 21 ---
DRUGS USED IN THE TREATMENT OF LEUKAEMIA TARGETED THERAPY: BCR‐ABL inhibitors: imatinib and nilotinib in CML Inhibitors of B cell signalling pathways: Ibrutinib, acalabrutinib Proteasome inhibitors: Bortezomib, Carfilzomib Monoclonal antibodies: Gemtuzumab ozogamicin (anti-CD33) Immunotherapy: Blinatumomab (BiTE- bispecific T-cell engager) Demethylation agents: Azacytidine, Decitabine
--- Slide 22 ---
DRUGS USED IN THE TREATMENT OF LEUKAEMIA OTHERS: Corticosteroids Asparaginase All Trans Retinoic acid (ATRA) Arsenic
--- Slide 23 ---
Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) HSCT is a novel therapy with great therapeutic potential in leukaemia It allows the substitution of malignant or damaged bone marrow with healthy Hematopoietic Stem Cells (HSC), restoring normal blood cell production, improving immune function and providing a potential ultimate cure to a significant number of patients
--- Slide 24 ---
HSCT Types of HSCT: Autologous SCT Allogeneic SCT Sources of Haematopoeitic stem cells (HSCs): Bone marrow Peripheral blood stem cells Cord blood
--- Slide 25 ---
HSCT Following remission induction with chemotherapy, HSCT is offered as a consolidation therapy It involves high dose chemotherapy +/- total body irradiation to eradicate leukaemia cells in the patient (conditioning) Stem cells are harvested from a suitably matched sibling donor or matched unrelated donor after HLA (tissue) typing
--- Slide 26 ---
HSCT Stem cells are infused in the recipient after conditioning with subsequent engraftment and reconstitution of the bone marrow HSCT offers graft versus leukaemia (GVL) effect and long-term remission and cure
--- Slide 27 ---
Chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapy CAR-T cell therapy is a revolutionary immunotherapy that transformed the treatment of relapsed/refractory B-cell malignancies and multiple myeloma Patients’ activated T cells are engineered (CAR) to target CD19 or BCMA-expressing tumour cells The CAR is able to latch on the CD19 or BCMA on cancer cells while enhancing the T cells’ ability to destroy the cancer cell
--- Slide 28 ---
Chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapy
--- Slide 29 ---
LEUKAEMIA ‘FIRSTS’ IN CANCER RESEARCH AND TREATMENT
--- Slide 30 ---
TREATMENT OF LEUKAEMIA The various novel therapies are used in combination as derived from well design clinical trials Example include the UKALL interim guidelines for treatment of ALL Drugs utilized in such protocols include dexamethasone, vincristine, Lasparaginase, methotrexate Targeted therapy like Imatinib is added to combination chemotherapy in BCR-ABL positive ALL
--- Slide 31 ---
CASE DISCUSSION 1 11-year-old girl She presented with wrist pains of 2 months, fever and body weakness Anaemia at presentation: Hb 8.2g/dL Blood film showed circulating monoblasts Immunophenotyping confirmed AML M5: CD13+CD33+CD34+CD64+HLADR+ Karyotyping: Normal FISH analysis: KMT2A rearrangement
--- Slide 32 ---
CASE DISCUSSION 1 TREATMENT: 2 CYCLES OF INDUCTION (7+3), (5+2) 2 CYCLE OF HIGH DOSE CYTARABINE (HIDAC) 1 CYCLE OF FLAG IDA (TRUNCATED, AKI) TARGET THERAPY: REVUMENIB + AZACYTIDINE + VENETOCLAX She succumbed following CNS relapse
--- Slide 33 ---
CASE DISCUSSION 2 48-year-old man He presented with a 6-month history of recurrent fevers and generalized body weakness. FBC at presentation showed Hb 11.0g/dL, leucocytosis 80,000 and thrombocytopenia 10,000 Co-morbidity: Hypertension, coronary artery disease Immunophenotyping and FISH confirmed AML While on induction chemotherapy he developed chest pain ECG showed inferior lead segment elevations in keeping with acute coronary symdrome He was managed by the cardiologist
--- Slide 34 ---
CASE DISCUSSION 2 Complete 2 cycles of induction (7+3) and 1 cycle of HiDAC Tissue typing done on immediate family and his brother was found to be a compatible donor Had allogeneic stem transplantation (Allo-HSCT) He remains in remission 5 years post stem cell transplantation
--- Slide 35 ---

--- Slide 1 ---
ACUTE LEUKAEMIAS Dr. OYEDEJI O.A. ( FMCPath )
--- Slide 2 ---
DEFINITION/ INTRODUCTION Neoplasms of hematopoietic precursor cells, characterized by the accumulation of excess blasts in the bone marrow. Malignant proliferation and accumulation of immature haemopoietic cells. They are usually of rapid onset & are rapidly fatal. They are subdivided into acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) and acute myeloblastic leukaemia (AML). ALL and AML can be further classified into subtypes
--- Slide 3 ---
CLINICAL FEATURES
--- Slide 4 ---
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF CLINICAL FEATURES Symptoms onset over days to weeks typically Pathophysiology follows: 1. Marrow failure due to infiltration/ replacement of normal marrow elements anaemia: fatigue, pallor thrombocytopenia: bleeding, spontaneous bruising neutropenia: infections, sepsis
--- Slide 5 ---
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF CLINICAL FEATURES 2. Infiltration of other organs - liver, spleen, lymph nodes (particularly in ALL): - hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, mediastinal masses (T-ALL) - gums: -gum hypertrophy ( monocytic subtype of AML) - bone pain especially in children with ALL any organ or tissue: - skin - leukemia cutis (AML) - soft tissue – chloromas - testis - CNS - solid organs
--- Slide 6 ---
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF CLINICAL FEATURES 3. leukostasis (only seen with WBC >> 50 x 10 9 /L) - CNS: -strokes lungs: -pulmonary infiltrates, hypoxemia 4. Constitutional symptoms - fevers, sweats are common weight loss uncommon 5. Other - exposure to substances that can initiate coagulation can cause DIC
--- Slide 7 ---
ACUTE LEUKAEMIA PATHOPHYSIOLOGY Acquired somatic mutations (chromosomal translocations and other genetic abnormalities) in early haematopoietic precursors → Clonal proliferation of a lymphoid or myeloid stem cell line and arrest in cell differentiation and maturation in early stages of hematopoiesis → Rapid proliferation of abnormal and dysfunctional blasts (with impaired apoptosis pathways) → Accumulation of leukaemic white blood cells in the bone marrow → Disrupted normal haematopoiesis → Leukocytosis/leukopenia (↑ risk of infections), thrombocytopenia (↑ bleeding), and anaemia .
--- Slide 8 ---
ACUTE LEUKAEMIA PATHOPHYSIOLOGY Immature blasts enter the bloodstream → Infiltration of other organs (particularly liver, spleen, lymph nodes, but also testes, skin, and mediastinum)
--- Slide 9 ---
LABORATORY & DIAGNOSTIC INVESTIGATIONS Approach Initial tests: CBC and peripheral blood smear (determine WBC count and the presence of blasts) Confirmatory test: bone marrow aspiration and biopsy (examine morphology, histochemistry, cytogenetics, and immunophenotyping) Further tests: if organ involvement is suspected (e.g., imaging, CSF analysis, biochemistry – renal and liver function tests etc )
--- Slide 10 ---
LABORATORY FEATURES Haematologic indices: Complete blood count Leukocytes: The white blood cell count (WBC) may be elevated, normal, or low and is not a reliable diagnostic marker. Thrombocytopenia Anaemia – usually normocytic Peripheral blood smear: presence of blasts Coagulation studies: rule out DIC, especially in the AML subtype promyelocytic leukaemia .
--- Slide 11 ---
LABORATORY FEATURES Features of acute leukaemia on bone marrow: Hypercellular marrow Excess number of blasts (Acute Leukaemia is diagnosed when over 20% of nucleated cells in the bone marrow are blasts.) NOTE: Although blasts are often readily identifiable in the peripheral blood, the key investigation to diagnose acute leukaemia before committing the patient to chemotherapy is the bone marrow investigation.
--- Slide 12 ---
LABORATORY FEATURES Bone marrow aspiration & biopsy is also helpful to: Sub-classify acute leukaemia Obtain samples for cytogenetic analysis These have prognostic value in addition to diagnostic value
--- Slide 13 ---
LABORATORY FEATURES Other lab findings: Electrolytes and metabolic markers: ↑ PO 4 2- ↓ Ca 2+ ↑ K + ↑ Lactate dehydrogenase and ↑uric acid indicate increased cell lysis X-ray may show lytic bone lesions and mediastinal mass due to enlargement of the thymus and/or mediastinal lymph nodes in ALL.
--- Slide 14 ---
DISTINCTION BETWEEN ALL AND AML Light microscopy - morphology - AML blasts: Auer rods, cytoplasmic granules helpful if present. - ALL blasts do not have Auer rods or granules. Special stains (cytochemistry) Flow cytometry (Immunophenotyping) Molecular techniques (Cytogenetics) Next-generation sequencing (NGS)
--- Slide 15 ---
DISTINCTION BETWEEN ALL AND AML
--- Slide 17 ---
ACUTE LYMPHOID LEUKAEMIA (ALL) A malignant transformation of a clone of lymphoid stem cells leading to a proliferation and accumulation of lymphoblasts . ALL can occur in both adults and children. It is the most common malignancy of childhood, constituting about 80% of childhood leukaemias .
--- Slide 18 ---
ALL - Aetiology No identifiable cause or risk factors in most cases Environmental risk factors - prior bone marrow damage due to alkylating chemotherapy, ionizing radiation and electromagnetic fields Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma is linked to infection with HTLV Genetic or chromosomal factors Down syndrome - risk of ALL is 10–20 times higher in patients with Down syndrome Neurofibromatosis type 1 Ataxia telangiectasia
--- Slide 19 ---
ALL Classification Classification may be based on Morphology - French-American-British (FAB) historical classification of ALL Immunophenotype classification of ALL (The WHO Classification): based on the origin (B cell or T cell) and maturity of the leukaemic cells. - The immunophenotype is determined by laboratory tests, including flow cytometry and cytogenetic tests.
--- Slide 20 ---
ALL Morphologic classification (FAB) L1 : Blasts are homogenous, small, with scant nucleoli and high nucleo -cytoplasmic ratio. (20-30% ALL) L2: Blasts are larger, heterogeneous with prominent nucleoli and more abundant cytoplasm (70% ALL) L3 : Blasts are large with basophilic cytoplasm and cytoplasmic vacuoles (1-3% ALL)
--- Slide 22 ---
ALL – Morphology (FAB L1)
--- Slide 23 ---
ALL – Morphology (FAB L3)
--- Slide 24 ---
ALL - Immunologic classification 1. Precursor B-cell types Pro B (CD 10 - ) Early Pre B (CD 10 + ) Also called common ALL or cALLA . It is common in children. Pre B (CD 10 +/- , intracytoplaasmic μ + ) 2. B-cell ALL - surface immunoglobulin (Sig + ) – related to Burkitt’s lymphoma (Mature B-cell ALL) 3. T-cell ALL - (CD3/ CD7 + ) – Adolescent males, thymic mass Early (pro-T) ALL Intermediate-T ALL Mature T-cell ALL
--- Slide 25 ---
ALL – WHO classification 1. B-lymphoblastic leukaemia / Lymphoma B-ALL with BCR::ABL1 (Philadelphia chromosome) B-ALL with ETV6::RUNX1 (t(12;21)) B-ALL with hyperdiploidy or hypodiploidy B-ALL with KMT2A rearrangement B-ALL with iAMP21 (intrachromosomal amplification of chromosome 21) B-ALL with DUX4, ZNF384, or PAX5 alterations B-ALL, NOS (not otherwise specified) 2. T-lymphoblastic Leukaemia / Lymphoma Includes all T-lineage ALLs with typical T-cell immunophenotype. T-ALL now includes molecular subtypes but not yet fully subclassified as in B-ALL.
--- Slide 27 ---
ALL - Incidence Common in children with incidence highest at 3 – 7 years. The cALL , early pre-B (CD10+) is most usual in children and has equal sex incidence. T – ALL has a male preponderance. In adults, the peak incidence is in those older than 65 years.
--- Slide 28 ---
ALL - Clinical Features The abnormal proliferation of malignant cells infiltrate the bone marrow and cause : Bone Marrow failure anaemia : – pallor, dyspnoea , tiredness Neutropaenia : – fever, malaise, infections- throat, skin, mouth, chest etc. Thrombocytopaenia : – spontaneous bruises, purpura, bleeding gums, menorrhagia Organ infiltration:– tender bones due to deposition of malignant cells in the periosteum, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly & meningeal symptoms such as headache, nausea, vomiting, & blurring of vision. Constitutional symptoms:- weight loss, night sweats
--- Slide 29 ---
Laboratory investigations Haematology – Full Blood Count ESR Reticulocyte count Blood film examination which may show normochromic normocytic cells, thrombocytopaenia and leukocytosis. Bone Marrow Aspiration & Biopsy – Blast cells >20% Cytochemical staining: - Strongly positive PAS stain and negative sudan black & peroxidase reaction.
--- Slide 30 ---
ALL Cytochemistry
--- Slide 31 ---
Laboratory investigations Biochemical tests – increased lactate dehydrogenase, uric acid and phosphate. Renal and liver functions tests are performed as baseline investigations before treatment begins. Lumbar Puncture – increased pressure and CSF may contain leukaemic cells. Radiology – CT Scan/X-Ray may show lytic bone lesions and mediastinal mass due to enlargement of the thymus and/or mediastinal lymph nodes. Ultrasound may show organ infiltrates.
--- Slide 32 ---
ALL Cytogenetics
--- Slide 33 ---
ALL Immunophenotype Both T-ALL and B-ALL cells express TdT (terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase) a marker present early in T and B cell development. TdT is involved in somatic mutations of the T cell receptor ( TcR ) and immunoglobulin (Ig) genes. B-ALL variably expresses CD 10 (CALLA-Common ALL Antigen), and CD19, a pan-B cell marker. B-ALL cells do not express surface immunoglobulin except mature B-ALL. T-ALL cells variably express T-cell related antigens CD1a, CD7, CD4, and CD8, in addition to Tdt T-ALL cells do not express the T cell receptor on their surface.
--- Slide 37 ---
Differential diagnosis of ALL These include: - Acute myeloid leukaemia , Aplastic anaemia , Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) Marrow infiltration with other malignancies, Infections mononucleosis, Pertusis Juvenile rheumatoid arthritis.
--- Slide 38 ---
ALL Management Supportive, Definitive & Curative Supportive Administration of fluid, antibiotics, red cell and platelet transfusions. Manage side effects of drugs – antiemetics , nutritional support Allopurinol to prevent hyperuricemia and urate-induced nephropathy Initial therapy may be complicated by tumour lysis syndrome, which is characterised by rapid development of hyperuricaemia , hyperkalaemia , hyperphosphataemia , hypocalcaemia, uric acid nephropathy and acute renal failure. The patient should be given allopurinol before starting therapy and be well hydrated.
--- Slide 39 ---
ALL Management Definitive - divided into: 1. Induction therapy (Remission induction) – vincristine weekly and prednisolone daily. High dose chemotherapy Give until patient goes into full remission. Patient is clinically normal. Haematological values return to normal. Less than 5% blasts in the bone marrow. No blast in the peripheral blood.
--- Slide 40 ---
ALL Management 2. Consolidation /Intensification:- it makes use of high dose of multidrug therapy. Patient may need a lot of supportive care. Drugs include cytosine arabinoside , daunorubicin , vincristine etc. 3. Maintenance- 6-mercaptopurine, methotrexate for 2yrs in adults and girls and 3 yrs in males. 4. CNS prophylaxis: intrathecal methotrexate/ radiation. Curative treatment – Allogeneic Stem cell transplantation.
--- Slide 41 ---
ALL Prognosis ALL is curable in children but difficult to treat in adults. slides.text: ACUTE LEUKAEMIAS Dr. OYEDEJI O.A. ( FMCPath )

DEFINITION/ INTRODUCTION Neoplasms of hematopoietic precursor cells, characterized by the accumulation of excess blasts in the bone marrow. Malignant proliferation and accumulation of immature haemopoietic cells. They are usually of rapid onset & are rapidly fatal. They are subdivided into acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) and acute myeloblastic leukaemia (AML). ALL and AML can be further classified into subtypes
CLINICAL FEATURES

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF CLINICAL FEATURES Symptoms onset over days to weeks typically Pathophysiology follows: 1. Marrow failure due to infiltration/ replacement of normal marrow elements anaemia: fatigue, pallor thrombocytopenia: bleeding, spontaneous bruising neutropenia: infections, sepsis

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF CLINICAL FEATURES 2. Infiltration of other organs - liver, spleen, lymph nodes (particularly in ALL): - hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, mediastinal masses (T-ALL) - gums: -gum hypertrophy ( monocytic subtype of AML) - bone pain especially in children with ALL any organ or tissue: - skin - leukemia cutis (AML) - soft tissue – chloromas - testis - CNS - solid organs

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF CLINICAL FEATURES 3. leukostasis (only seen with WBC >> 50 x 10 9 /L) - CNS: -strokes lungs: -pulmonary infiltrates, hypoxemia 4. Constitutional symptoms - fevers, sweats are common weight loss uncommon 5. Other - exposure to substances that can initiate coagulation can cause DIC

ACUTE LEUKAEMIA PATHOPHYSIOLOGY Acquired somatic mutations (chromosomal translocations and other genetic abnormalities) in early haematopoietic precursors → Clonal proliferation of a lymphoid or myeloid stem cell line and arrest in cell differentiation and maturation in early stages of hematopoiesis → Rapid proliferation of abnormal and dysfunctional blasts (with impaired apoptosis pathways) → Accumulation of leukaemic white blood cells in the bone marrow → Disrupted normal haematopoiesis → Leukocytosis/leukopenia (↑ risk of infections), thrombocytopenia (↑ bleeding), and anaemia .
ACUTE LEUKAEMIA PATHOPHYSIOLOGY Immature blasts enter the bloodstream → Infiltration of other organs (particularly liver, spleen, lymph nodes, but also testes, skin, and mediastinum)

LABORATORY & DIAGNOSTIC INVESTIGATIONS Approach Initial tests: CBC and peripheral blood smear (determine WBC count and the presence of blasts) Confirmatory test: bone marrow aspiration and biopsy (examine morphology, histochemistry, cytogenetics, and immunophenotyping) Further tests: if organ involvement is suspected (e.g., imaging, CSF analysis, biochemistry – renal and liver function tests etc )

LABORATORY FEATURES Haematologic indices: Complete blood count Leukocytes: The white blood cell count (WBC) may be elevated, normal, or low and is not a reliable diagnostic marker. Thrombocytopenia Anaemia – usually normocytic Peripheral blood smear: presence of blasts Coagulation studies: rule out DIC, especially in the AML subtype promyelocytic leukaemia .

LABORATORY FEATURES Features of acute leukaemia on bone marrow: Hypercellular marrow Excess number of blasts (Acute Leukaemia is diagnosed when over 20% of nucleated cells in the bone marrow are blasts.) NOTE: Although blasts are often readily identifiable in the peripheral blood, the key investigation to diagnose acute leukaemia before committing the patient to chemotherapy is the bone marrow investigation.

LABORATORY FEATURES Bone marrow aspiration & biopsy is also helpful to: Sub-classify acute leukaemia Obtain samples for cytogenetic analysis These have prognostic value in addition to diagnostic value

LABORATORY FEATURES Other lab findings: Electrolytes and metabolic markers: ↑ PO 4 2- ↓ Ca 2+ ↑ K + ↑ Lactate dehydrogenase and ↑uric acid indicate increased cell lysis X-ray may show lytic bone lesions and mediastinal mass due to enlargement of the thymus and/or mediastinal lymph nodes in ALL.

DISTINCTION BETWEEN ALL AND AML Light microscopy - morphology - AML blasts: Auer rods, cytoplasmic granules helpful if present. - ALL blasts do not have Auer rods or granules. Special stains (cytochemistry) Flow cytometry (Immunophenotyping) Molecular techniques (Cytogenetics) Next-generation sequencing (NGS)
DISTINCTION BETWEEN ALL AND AML

ACUTE LYMPHOID LEUKAEMIA (ALL) A malignant transformation of a clone of lymphoid stem cells leading to a proliferation and accumulation of lymphoblasts . ALL can occur in both adults and children. It is the most common malignancy of childhood, constituting about 80% of childhood leukaemias .

ALL - Aetiology No identifiable cause or risk factors in most cases Environmental risk factors - prior bone marrow damage due to alkylating chemotherapy, ionizing radiation and electromagnetic fields Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma is linked to infection with HTLV Genetic or chromosomal factors Down syndrome - risk of ALL is 10–20 times higher in patients with Down syndrome Neurofibromatosis type 1 Ataxia telangiectasia

ALL Classification Classification may be based on Morphology - French-American-British (FAB) historical classification of ALL Immunophenotype classification of ALL (The WHO Classification): based on the origin (B cell or T cell) and maturity of the leukaemic cells. - The immunophenotype is determined by laboratory tests, including flow cytometry and cytogenetic tests.

ALL Morphologic classification (FAB) L1 : Blasts are homogenous, small, with scant nucleoli and high nucleo -cytoplasmic ratio. (20-30% ALL) L2: Blasts are larger, heterogeneous with prominent nucleoli and more abundant cytoplasm (70% ALL) L3 : Blasts are large with basophilic cytoplasm and cytoplasmic vacuoles (1-3% ALL)
ALL – Morphology (FAB L1)
ALL – Morphology (FAB L3)

Pre B (CD 10 +/- , intracytoplaasmic μ + ) 2. B-cell ALL - surface immunoglobulin (Sig + ) – related to Burkitt’s lymphoma (Mature B-cell ALL) 3. T-cell ALL - (CD3/ CD7 + ) – Adolescent males, thymic mass Early (pro-T) ALL Intermediate-T ALL Mature T-cell ALL

T-lymphoblastic Leukaemia / Lymphoma Includes all T-lineage ALLs with typical T-cell immunophenotype. T-ALL now includes molecular subtypes but not yet fully subclassified as in B-ALL.

Constitutional symptoms:- weight loss, night sweats

ALL Cytochemistry

Radiology – CT Scan/X-Ray may show lytic bone lesions and mediastinal mass due to enlargement of the thymus and/or mediastinal lymph nodes. Ultrasound may show organ infiltrates.

ALL Immunophenotype Both T-ALL and B-ALL cells express TdT (terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase) a marker present early in T and B cell development. TdT is involved in somatic mutations of the T cell receptor ( TcR ) and immunoglobulin (Ig) genes. B-ALL variably expresses CD 10 (CALLA-Common ALL Antigen), and CD19, a pan-B cell marker. B-ALL cells do not express surface immunoglobulin except mature B-ALL. T-ALL cells variably express T-cell related antigens CD1a, CD7, CD4, and CD8, in addition to Tdt T-ALL cells do not express the T cell receptor on their surface.

Differential diagnosis of ALL These include: - Acute myeloid leukaemia , Aplastic anaemia , Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) Marrow infiltration with other malignancies, Infections mononucleosis, Pertusis Juvenile rheumatoid arthritis.

ALL Management Supportive, Definitive & Curative Supportive Administration of fluid, antibiotics, red cell and platelet transfusions. Manage side effects of drugs – antiemetics , nutritional support Allopurinol to prevent hyperuricemia and urate-induced nephropathy Initial therapy may be complicated by tumour lysis syndrome, which is characterised by rapid development of hyperuricaemia , hyperkalaemia , hyperphosphataemia , hypocalcaemia, uric acid nephropathy and acute renal failure. The patient should be given allopurinol before starting therapy and be well hydrated.

ALL Management Definitive - divided into: 1. Induction therapy (Remission induction) – vincristine weekly and prednisolone daily. High dose chemotherapy Give until patient goes into full remission. Patient is clinically normal. Haematological values return to normal. Less than 5% blasts in the bone marrow. No blast in the peripheral blood.

ALL Management 2. Consolidation /Intensification:- it makes use of high dose of multidrug therapy. Patient may need a lot of supportive care. Drugs include cytosine arabinoside , daunorubicin , vincristine etc. 3. Maintenance- 6-mercaptopurine, methotrexate for 2yrs in adults and girls and 3 yrs in males. 4. CNS prophylaxis: intrathecal methotrexate/ radiation. Curative treatment – Allogeneic Stem cell transplantation.

ALL Prognosis ALL is curable in children but difficult to treat in adults. --- Slide 1 ---
CHRONIC LEUKAEMIAS Dr. OYEDEJI O.A. ( FMCPath )
--- Slide 3 ---
CHRONIC LEUKAEMIAS Slowly progressing malignancy that starts in blood-forming tissue and causes the production and accumulation of abnormal blood cells. Accumulated blood cells are matured white cells (cells in late stages of myeloid or lymphoid cell production). There are two main types: chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) and chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML), both of which primarily affect adults.
--- Slide 4 ---
CHRONIC LYMPHOCYTIC LEUKAEMIA (CLL) Monoclonal disorder characterized by a progressive accumulation of functionally incompetent lymphocytes - Characterized by chronic persistent lymphocytosis. All normal stages of lymphoid development are postulated to have a malignant counterpart. In the case of CLL, B-cell CLL derives from the antigen-experienced B cell. They express CD19, CD5 and CD23 and have reduced levels of membrane immunoglobulins ( IgM , IgD ), CD79b & FMC7. CLL cells are monoclonal because they express only one form of light chain (lambda or kappa) on their cell surface.
--- Slide 5 ---
CHRONIC LYMPHOCYTIC LEUKAEMIA (CLL) B cell CLL is characterized by a progressive accumulation within the marrow and blood of long-lived mature leukaemic lymphocytes due to: stimulation of growth by external signals e.g cytokines, chemokines & ligands binding to B cell receptors, and due to reduced apoptosis (programmed cell death) felt to be largely mediated by overexpression of bcl-2, a protein known to inhibit cellular apoptosis. Thus, it is due to inappropriately prolonged survival of the cells, not because of rapid production Much less is known about T-CLL as this is a rare disease.
--- Slide 6 ---
CLL - Epidemiology B-CLL is the most common form of leukaemia in the western hemisphere 25-30% of all leukaemias . The peak incidence of CLL is in the 6th decade of life. The overall incidence is 20 per 100,000 in persons >70 years of age. The male to female ratio is 2:1. 95% of CLL is of B cell origin. T-CLL is a rare disease.
--- Slide 7 ---
CLL - Epidemiology Overall median survival of patients is about 10 to 20 years. Individual prognosis can be quite variable – indolent in some patients and life expectancy is not shortened, aggressive in others and can progress rapidly and survival from diagnosis may be 2-3 years. Mortality often due to: overwhelming tumour burden with marked adenopathy and splenomegaly Overwhelming infection bleeding, and transformation to an aggressive lymphoma, so called a Richter’s transformation.
--- Slide 8 ---
CLL – Clinical features Incidental finding on CBC, where there is isolated lymphocytosis, and the patient is asymptomatic. If complaints are present, they are usually: weakness, easy fatigue, night sweats, fever and weight loss. There may be frequent bacterial and viral infections because of hypogammaglobulinemia . Patients with CLL may report an exaggerated response to mosquito or other insect bites.
--- Slide 9 ---
CLL – Clinical features On physical examination, symmetrical peripheral lymphadenopathy is most frequent abnormal finding involving the neck, axillae and inguinal regions. Nodes are usually painless. Splenomegaly and hepatomegaly are variably present. Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA) and immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) are associated with CLL and can result in severe anaemia and thrombocytopenia. AIHA occurs 10-25% of the time, while ITP is seen in 2% of patients. AIHA, ITP, hypogammaglobulinemia and an exaggerated response to mosquito bites result from the immune dysregulation which occurs in CLL.
--- Slide 10 ---
Lymph gland involvement may be subtle or spectacular, but generally it is only within nodes: unsightly or uncomfortable; but not invasive Accumulation in lymph glands
--- Slide 11 ---
CLL – Laboratory findings Lymphocytosis: diagnosis of CLL requires evidence of lymphocytosis, at least 10 × 10 9 /L, and lymphocytic infiltration in the bone marrow of at least 40%. With immunological methods, particularly the detection of monoclonal B-cell populations by light-chain restriction, it is possible to diagnose the disease with lymphocyte counts below this threshold. ( Absolute clonal B cell lymphocyte count >5 × 10 9 /L) 30% of CLL patients have anaemia or thrombocytopenia secondary to an immune process or marrow infiltration.
--- Slide 12 ---
CLL – Laboratory findings Morphologically, the lymphocytes in blood films are small and show scanty cytoplasm and a characteristic pattern of nuclear chromatin clumping, nucleolus is inconspicuous - CLL cells indistinguishable from normal lymphocytes. Azurophil granules are seen only in a minority of normal T cells. The presence of smudge/smear cells, literally flattened, destroyed cells on a regular blood smear, is consistently seen with CLL
--- Slide 13 ---
CLL – Laboratory findings Peripheral film usually shows normocytic normochromic anaemia in later stages. If AIHA is present, spherocytes and polychromasia can be seen on the blood smear. Bone marrow: cellularity is increased (number of cells seen) and 30-99% of nucleated cells are mature lymphocytes.
--- Slide 14 ---
Note the cells are small and mature compared with typical “blast cells” CLL What they look like AML
--- Slide 15 ---
As cells are small, non-functional and largely “inert”, CLL in blood counts of 50x109/l (or more) are often without symptoms Incidental finding
--- Slide 16 ---
CLL – Laboratory findings Immunophenotyping : CLL cells co-express CD19 and CD5 . CD19 is a B cell marker, and CD5 is a T-cell marker. The expression of a T cell marker on a B cell is an example of lineage infidelity that is seen not only in CLL but in AML and ALL as well. CLL cells are also positive for CD23, negative for CD79b (or dim+) They are either kappa or lambda light chain restricted ( ie . express only one or the other light chain) and have a dim level of expression of the immunoglobulin heavy chains IgM and IgD .
--- Slide 17 ---
CLL – Laboratory findings The normal T-cell/B-cell ratio is reversed in CLL. Normally, T lymphocytes constitute approximately 80% of the total lymphoid population and B lymphocytes, 20% of the lymphoid cells. In B-cell CLL, B cells account for nearly 90% of all lymphocytes.
--- Slide 18 ---
CLL – Laboratory findings Cytogenetics and molecular diagnostics are not needed to make the diagnosis of CLL. However, they are useful in determining the survival of patients. In particular, 17p deletions, corresponding to a mutation in the p53 gene, are associated with very short survival, as are 11q deletions. Other markers of poor prognosis include the presence of the p53 mutation (with or without chromosome deletions), and an unmutated Vh gene. Vh corresponds to the variable portion of the immunoglobulin heavy chain.
--- Slide 19 ---

CHRONIC LEUKAEMIAS Slowly progressing malignancy that starts in blood-forming tissue and causes the production and accumulation of abnormal blood cells. Accumulated blood cells are matured white cells (cells in late stages of myeloid or lymphoid cell production). There are two main types: chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) and chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML), both of which primarily affect adults.

CHRONIC LYMPHOCYTIC LEUKAEMIA (CLL) Monoclonal disorder characterized by a progressive accumulation of functionally incompetent lymphocytes - Characterized by chronic persistent lymphocytosis. All normal stages of lymphoid development are postulated to have a malignant counterpart. In the case of CLL, B-cell CLL derives from the antigen-experienced B cell. They express CD19, CD5 and CD23 and have reduced levels of membrane immunoglobulins ( IgM , IgD ), CD79b & FMC7. CLL cells are monoclonal because they express only one form of light chain (lambda or kappa) on their cell surface.

CHRONIC LYMPHOCYTIC LEUKAEMIA (CLL) B cell CLL is characterized by a progressive accumulation within the marrow and blood of long-lived mature leukaemic lymphocytes due to: stimulation of growth by external signals e.g cytokines, chemokines & ligands binding to B cell receptors, and due to reduced apoptosis (programmed cell death) felt to be largely mediated by overexpression of bcl-2, a protein known to inhibit cellular apoptosis. Thus, it is due to inappropriately prolonged survival of the cells, not because of rapid production Much less is known about T-CLL as this is a rare disease.

CLL - Epidemiology B-CLL is the most common form of leukaemia in the western hemisphere 25-30% of all leukaemias . The peak incidence of CLL is in the 6th decade of life. INTRODUCTION What are Leukaemias ? Malignant neoplasm of the haemopoietic tissue, characterized by replacement of the normal bone marrow elements with abnormal blood cells. Generalized malignant neoplastic proliferation or accumulation of leukopoietic cells in the bone marrow with or without involvement of the peripheral blood. A group of disorders characterized by the proliferation and/or accumulation of malignant white cells in the bone marrow and blood.
--- Slide 4 ---
INTRODUCTION Recall normal haemopoiesis - Abnormality can occur at any stage in the maturation sequence and lead to a variety of leukaemic illnesses which are classified according to the developmental stage affected.
--- Slide 5 ---
INTRODUCTION
--- Slide 8 ---
LEUKAEMIA AETIOLOGY PRINCIPLES The neoplastic cell is a hematopoietic pleuripotent stem cell, or a committed stem cell - lymphoid or myeloid commitment. Leukemogenesis is characterized by dysregulation of cell growth, cell differentiation, or cell death, associated with genetic mutations - proliferation of the leukemic clone. When differentiation is blocked at an early stage - accumulation of blasts and the clinical consequences. Cell death blocked – accumulation of matured cells
--- Slide 9 ---
LEUKAEMIA AETIOLOGY PRINCIPLES The TWO-HIT MODEL OF LEUKEMOGENESIS posits that acute leukemias arise from two (or more) derangements of genes that regulate haematopoietic differentiation and proliferation. Neither mutation alone is sufficient to generate the acute leukaemia phenotype.
--- Slide 11 ---
LEUKAEMIA AETIOLOGY No known causes of leukaemia but certain factors are associated with the aetiology. A combination of Genetic background (Chromosomal alterations) Host factors Environmental influence determines the risk of developing leukaemia in most cases. However, in some cases neither genetic susceptibility nor environmental agent is apparent
--- Slide 12 ---
LEUKAEMIA AETIOLOGY - Genetic Chromosomal alterations : Mutations are common in leukaemias and mainly affect three classes of normal regulatory genes - Growth-promoting oncogenes - mutation leads to abnormal cell proliferation Growth-inhibiting tumour suppressor genes - mutation removes the molecular brake leading to uncontrolled proliferation Genes that regulate programmed cell death or apoptosis - mutation causes excessive cell accumulation.
--- Slide 13 ---
LEUKAEMIA AETIOLOGY - Genetic The genetic damage that activates oncogenes or inactivates tumour suppressor genes may be subtle ( e.g point mutation) or large enough to be detected in a karyotype. The common types of structural abnormalities in tumour cells are: Translocation Point mutation Deletion Gene amplification. Whole chromosomes may be gained or lost
--- Slide 14 ---
LEUKAEMIA AETIOLOGY - Genetic Translocations are extremely common in haemopoietic neoplasms. Most notable is Philadephia (Ph 1 ) in CML. In Philadelphia chromosome, part of chromosome 9 is transferred to chromosome 22 and vice versa hence there is reciprocal translocation between both chromosomes which results in leukaemia . This cytogenetic change is seen in 90% of cases of CML. Point Mutation : Mutation within the RAS oncogene
--- Slide 15 ---
LEUKAEMIA AETIOLOGY - Genetic Deletions are the second most prevalent abnormality in tumour cells. Deletion of chromosome 20q is the most common chromosomal abnormality in polycythaemia rubra vera . Gene Amplification is the process by which the number of copies of a chromosome segment is increased in a somatic cell. This is very rare in haematologic malignancies.
--- Slide 16 ---
Haemopoietic Stem Cell (HSC) Mutations increase with age -isolated HSC and sequenced cells -takes blood from 2 cords for people from 20, 30, 40, 50, 70 yrs of age -as you age, number of mutations increase per HSC
--- Slide 17 ---
LEUKAEMIA AETIOLOGY - Host 2. Host Factors i. Heredity: Heredity plays an important role in leukaemias . Identical twins (have 25% chance), Fraternal twins (less chance). ii. Congenital chromosomal abnormalities: Patients with these illnesses have a higher chance of having acute leukaemias . Down’s Syndrome – 40% chance of AML, increased incidence of ALL Klinefelter syndrome
--- Slide 18 ---
LEUKAEMIA AETIOLOGY - Host Turners Syndrome Fanconi’s anaemia Bloom’s Syndrome iii. Immunodeficiency: Anything that disturbs the immune surveillance may lead to development of leukaemias because the protection has been removed. iv. Chronic Marrow dysfunction e.g. Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), clonal blood disorder such as aplastic anaemia & PNH.
--- Slide 19 ---
LEUKAEMIA AETIOLOGY - Host Haematologic disorders predisposing to acute leukaemia CML and other myeloproliferative disorders (PRV, ET, MF) Myelodysplastic syndromes Aplastic anaemia Multiple myeloma, Waldenström’s macroglobulinaemia Paroxysmal Nocturnal Haemoglobinuria (PNH) Acute leukaemia arising out of hematologic disorders is more frequently AML than ALL
--- Slide 20 ---
LEUKAEMIA AETIOLOGY - Environmental 3. Environmental Factors: Ionizing radiations – Malignancy may develop following repeated exposure to heavy ionising radiations e.g. Radiotherapy, X-ray e.g. in a pregnant woman – leukaemia may develop in the foetus . So also, are victims of Atomic bombs who later developed leukaemia . Chemicals & drugs – Certain drugs are known to predispose to secondary malignancies like leukaemias .
--- Slide 21 ---
LEUKAEMIA AETIOLOGY - Environmental Some of these drugs are used to treat malignancy e.g. Busulphan , chlorambucil which are alkylating agents. Certain chemicals e.g. Benzene containing chemicals like petroleum products have also been implicated. Viruses: – Can directly cause leukaemias . It is now known that retroviruses especially the C-type RNA viruses can cause leukaemias . These viruses possess the reverse transcriptase enzyme. HTLV-1 - Human T cell Leukaemia/Lymphoma Virus can cause T-cell ALL but not AML.
--- Slide 22 ---
LEUKAEMIA CLASSIFICATION Main classification is into 2 groups based on: The stage of cell maturation at which the abnormalities occur: Acute and Chronic leukaemia The lineage of cells affected: Myeloid and Lymphoid Each group whether Acute or Chronic is subdivided into 2 based on the lineage of cells affected – Myeloid or Lymphoid.
--- Slide 23 ---
LEUKAEMIA CLASSIFICATION
--- Slide 24 ---
ACUTE LEUKAEMIAS Acute leukaemias - usually aggressive diseases in which malignant transformation occurs in the haemopoietic stem cells or early progenitors There is usually: increased rate of proliferation reduced apoptosis and block in cellular differentiation. These lead to accumulation in the bone marrow of early haemopoietic cells known as blast cells. They are usually of rapid onset & are rapidly fatal. Subdivided into acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) and acute myeloblastic leukaemia (AML).
--- Slide 25 ---
CHRONIC LEUKAEMIAS Distinguished from acute leukaemias by their slower progression with the predominant cell type showing maturity. Excessive build-up of relatively mature, but still abnormal white blood cells. Typically takes months or years to progress. Chronic leukaemias are sometimes monitored for some time before treatment to ensure maximum effectiveness of therapy. Chronic leukaemia mostly occurs in older people. Chronic leukaemias can be broadly subdivided into myeloid and lymphoid groups.
--- Slide 26 ---
LEUKAEMIA CLASSIFICATION FEATURES
--- Slide 27 ---
LEUKAEMIAS
--- Slide 28 ---
LEUKAEMIA CLINICAL FEATURES
--- Slide 29 ---
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF CLINICAL FEATURES Symptoms onset over days to weeks typically Pathophysiology follows: 1. Marrow failure due to infiltration/ replacement of normal marrow elements anaemia: fatigue, pallor thrombocytopenia: bleeding, spontaneous bruising neutropenia: infections, sepsis
--- Slide 30 ---
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF CLINICAL FEATURES 2. Infiltration of other organs - liver, spleen, lymph nodes (particularly in ALL): - hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, mediastinal masses (T-ALL) - gums: -gum hypertrophy ( monocytic subtype of AML) - bone pain esp. in children with ALL - any organ or tissue: - skin - leukaemia cutis (AML) - soft tissue – chloromas - testis - CNS - solid organs
--- Slide 31 ---
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF CLINICAL FEATURES 3. Leukostasis (only seen with WBC >> 50 x 10 9 /L) - CNS: strokes - lungs: pulmonary infiltrates, hypoxemia 4. Constitutional symptoms - fevers, sweats are common weight loss 5. Others: - e.g. exposure to substances that can initiate coagulation can cause DIC
--- Slide 32 ---
LABORATORY & DIAGNOSTIC INVESTIGATIONS Approach Initial tests: CBC and peripheral blood smear (determine WBC count and the presence/ absence of blasts) Confirmatory test: bone marrow aspiration and biopsy (examine morphology, histochemistry, cytogenetics, and immunophenotyping) Further tests: if organ involvement is suspected (e.g., imaging, CSF analysis, biochemistry – renal and liver function tests, etc.)
--- Slide 33 ---
LABORATORY FEATURES Haematologic indices: Complete blood count Leukocytes: The white blood cell count (WBC) may be elevated, normal, or low and is not a reliable diagnostic marker. Thrombocytopenia Anaemia – usually normocytic Peripheral blood smear: presence or absence of blasts Coagulation studies: rule out DIC, especially in the AML subtype promyelocytic leukaemia .
--- Slide 34 ---
LABORATORY FEATURES Bone marrow aspiration & biopsy are also helpful for: Sub-classifying acute leukaemia Obtain samples for cytogenetic analysis These have prognostic value in addition to the diagnostic value.
--- Slide 35 ---
LABORATORY FEATURES Other lab findings: Electrolytes and metabolic markers: ↑ PO 4 2- ↓ Ca 2+ ↑ K + ↑ Lactate dehydrogenase and ↑uric acid indicate increased cell lysis X-ray may show lytic bone lesions and mediastinal mass due to enlargement of the thymus and/or mediastinal lymph nodes in ALL.
--- Slide 36 ---

parsed.text:
--- Slide 1 ---
HODGKIN’S LYMPHOMA Dr Ademola Adewoyin lECTURER /consultant haematologist
--- Slide 2 ---
HD: Definition Neoplastic disorder with development of specific infiltrate containing pathologic Reed-Sternberg (RS) cells. It usually arises in lymph nodes and spreads to contiguous groups. Extra-nodal presentation are rare. Disease is associated with defective cellular immunity .
--- Slide 3 ---
Hodgkin’s Disease Background first described in 1832 by Dr. Thomas Hodgkin characterized by the presence of Reed-Sternberg cells multinucleated giant cells described by Sternberg in 1898 and Reed in 1902 classified as an infectious disease until 1950’s
--- Slide 4 ---
Thomas Hodgkin (1798-1866) Thomas Hodgkin published in 1832 the first description of lymphoma, specifically of the form named after him, Hodgkin's lymphoma. Name Hodgkin's Disease proposed in 1865 by Wiks.
--- Slide 5 ---
Characteristics of HD Usually arise in LNs, preferentially cervical region Majority manifest clinically in the young Neoplastic tissues usually contain a small number of scattered large mono-nucleated and multi-nucleated tumor cells designated Hodgkin and Reed- sternberge cells or HRS cells) The tumor cells are often ringed by T-lymphocytes in a rosette -like manner In contrast with NHL where there had been a steady increase in incidence, the absolute incidence of HD has not apparently changed.
--- Slide 6 ---
HL: Histology Reed-Sternberg cells (or RS variants) in the affected tissues cell of origin: germinal centre B-cell most cells in affected lymph node are polyclonal reactive lymphoid cells, not neoplastic cells
--- Slide 7 ---
Reed-Sternberg cell
--- Slide 8 ---
Epidemiology
--- Slide 9 ---
Hodgkin’s Disease: Epidemiology 14% of malignant lymphomas 0.5% of all malignancies Highly treatable and curable even when disseminated.
--- Slide 10 ---
Hodgkin’s Disease: Epidemiology men > women whites > blacks > Asians no clear risk factors, several implicated EBV (pathogen or passenger) HIV woodworking, farming rare familial aggregations
--- Slide 11 ---
Epidemiology bimodal age distribution : 15-35 years and above 50 years male predominance M:F = 1.7:1 More common in affluent families with few siblings. In developing countries, more common in young children
--- Slide 12 ---
Etiology
--- Slide 13 ---
Etiology of Hodgkin’s Disease/ Associated (etiological?) factors Reed-Sternberg cells are the malignant cells. Minor population in the malignant tissues many normal lymphocytes, eosinophils, other cells Cell of origin is now known to be of B cell origin. Some R-S cells contain EBV genomes indicating EBV infection smaller family size higher socio-economic status caucasian > non- caucasian ?possible genetic predisposition other: HIV? occupation? herbicides?
--- Slide 14 ---
A possible model of pathogenesis germinal centre B cell transforming event(s) loss of apoptosis RS cell inflammatory response EBV? cytokines
--- Slide 15 ---
Reed-Sternberg Cell
--- Slide 16 ---
Clinical Presentation .
--- Slide 17 ---
Clinical Presentation Non-tender lymph nodes enlargement ( localised ) neck and supraclavicular area 60-80% mediastinal adenopathy 50% other ( abdominal, extranodal disease ) systemic symptoms (B symptoms) 30% unexplained fever unexplained night sweats unexplained weight loss (10% per 6 months) other symptoms fatigue, weakness, pruritus cough , chest pain, shortness of breath, vena cava syndrome abdominal pain, bowel disturbances, ascites bone pain
--- Slide 18 ---
Other Signs and Symptoms Pel-Ebstein fever. relapsing, high-grade fever that can reach 105-106°F, periodicity of 7-10 days. Fever spikes abrupt in onset and resolution Pain on drinking alcohol. Pel-Ebstein Fever
--- Slide 19 ---
Clinical Features T cell mediated immune deficiency, even in early stage disease. Prone to infections: Herpes zoster (“shingles”) in one fourth of patients Fungal or mycobacterial infections Immune defect may persist even after lymphoma is cured. Predictable contiguous spread of disease: cervical nodes to mediastinum or axilla mediastinum to para- otic nodes or spleen, etc. Basis for staging and treatment decisions.
--- Slide 20 ---
Diagnosis .
--- Slide 21 ---
Diagnosis Excisional biopsy of a lymph node. Fine needle aspirate is not sufficient to make the diagnosis of Hodgkin’s disease. Same as for non-Hodgkin’s: Hx + PE, labs, CT scans, bone marrow biopsy PLUS: Gallium scan Lymphangiogram or staging laparotomy can be done ONLY if results would affect treatment decisions
--- Slide 22 ---
Diagnosis of Hodgkin Disease is based on microscopic examination of lymph node or other involved tissue it requires identification of diagnostic Reed-Sternberg cells
--- Slide 23 ---
Classification
--- Slide 24 ---
Classification Comprised of two disease entities Nodular Lymphocyte Predominant Hodgkin Lymphoma[NLPHD] Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma[CHL] They distinctly defer in their clinical features and behavior as well as the composition of their cellular background
--- Slide 25 ---
Hodgkin Lymphoma Classification “Classic” Hodgkin’s Disease nodular sclerosis mixed cellularity lymphocyte depleted (very rare) classical lymphocyte rich HRS cells CD30 and CD15 positive nodular lymphocyte predominant HRS cells (L&H cells) have B cell markers CD 20 and surface Immunoglobulin
--- Slide 26 ---
Hodgkin’s Disease Approach to the Patient staging evaluation Hx & PE CBC, diff, plts ESR, LDH, albumin, LFT’s, Cr CT scans chest/abd/pelvis bone marrow evaluation **PET or gallium scan** **lymphangiogram or laparotomy**
--- Slide 28 ---
Subtypes of Hodgkin’s Disease NOTE Unlike non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, in Hodgkin’s Disease the histologic subtype does not determine how the disease is treated.
--- Slide 29 ---
Staging Classification Ann Arbor modified by Cotswolds Stage I: involvement of single lymph node region or lymphoid structure Stage II: involvement of two or more lymph node regions on same side of diaphragm Stage III: involvement of lymph node regions or structures on both sides of diaphragm III 1 : with splenic hilar,celiac,portal nodes III 2 : with para-aortic,iliac,mesenteric nodes Stage IV: involvement of extranodal site(s) A. Asymptomatic B. Symptomatic (B symptoms) X. Bulky disease ( > 1/3 widening of mediastinum, > 10cm max.dimension of nodal mass) E. Involvement of a single, localised, extranodal site
--- Slide 30 ---
Ann Arbor Staging System for Hodgkin's Disease and Non-Hodgkin's Lymphoma Stage I Stage II Stage III Stage IV Reprinted with permission. Adapted from Skarin. Dana-Farber Cancer Institute Atlas of Diagnostic Oncology . 1991.
--- Slide 31 ---
Modified Ann Arbor Staging “E” designation for extranodal disease B symptoms recurrent drenching night sweats during previous month unexplained, persistent, or recurrent fever with temps above 38 C during the previous month unexplained weight loss of more than 10% of the body weight during the previous 6 months Criteria for bulk 10 cm nodal mass mediastinal mass > 1/3 thorax diameter
--- Slide 32 ---
Staging evaluation for Hodgkin’s Disease (1) Essential pathologic documentation by hemopathologist physical examination documentation of B symptoms laboratory evaluation complete blood count, ESR liver function tests renal function tests lactate dehydrogenase chest radiograph ultrasonography CT scan of chest, abdomen and pelvis bone marrow aspiration / biopsy (bilateral)
--- Slide 33 ---
Staging evaluation for Hodgkin’s Disease (2) Essential under certain circumstances liver biopsy gallium scan technetium bone scan bone radiographs MRI bipedal lymphangiogram staging laparotomy Useful but not essential tests cell-surface marker phenotypic analysis gene rearrangement analysis
--- Slide 34 ---
Treatment .
--- Slide 35 ---
Treatment of Hodgkin Disesae (1) With appropriate treatment about 85% of patients with Hodgkin disease are curable I A,B: Radiation therapy II A : combination chemotherapy + Radiotherapy IIB; IIIA, B; IV A,B : combination chemotherapy (+/- radiotherapy)
--- Slide 36 ---
Treatment of Hodgkin Disesae (2) Radiation therapy mantle field paraaortic field pelvic field dose: 35-40 Gy/T Combination chemotherapy ABVD BEACOPP
--- Slide 37 ---
Treatment and Prognosis Stage Treatment Failure-free survival Overall 5 year survival I,II ABVD x 4 & radiation 70-80% 80-90% III,IV ABVD x 6 60-70% 70-80%
--- Slide 38 ---
Hodgkin Lymphoma Adverse prognostic features for stage I & II (EORTC data) more than 3 nodal sites bulky adenopathy ESR > 50 B symptoms invasion into critical organs male age > 40 MC or LD subtype should probably not receive XRT alone if any of the above present (excessive relapse rate)
--- Slide 39 ---
Hodgkin Lymphoma Independent adverse prognostic factors advanced stage (III-IV) male sex age > 45 albumin < 4 gm/dl HgB < 10.5 mg/dl stage IV disease WBC count > 15,000/mm 3 lymphocyte count < 600/mm 3 (Hasenclever et al, NEJM 339,1506-1514;1998)
--- Slide 40 ---
Hodgkin’s Disease Results of Treatment stage 5 year overall survival I 90% II 90% III 80% IV 65%
--- Slide 41 ---
Chemotherapy Regimens MOPP M echlorethamine, O ncovin, P rocarbazine, P rednisone ABVD A driamycin, B leomycin, V inblastine, D acarbazine BEACOPP Bleomycin, Etoposide, Adriamycin, Cyclophos, Oncovin,Pred, Procarbacin
--- Slide 42 ---
Treatment Options Often, patients who relapse after radiotherapy can be cured by salvage chemotherapy. Combined chemotherapy and radiotherapy is given for bulky mediastinal masses. Chemotherapy now being tested for earlier stages of the disease.
--- Slide 43 ---
Late Complications of Hodgkin’s Disease High incidence of second malignancies leukemia first 10 years, solid tumors over time. Leukemia in patients receiving alkylating agents or combined chemo/XRT. Lung cancer and breast cancer in patients receiving XRT to chest. Lung cancer especially high in smokers.
--- Slide 44 ---
Long term complications of treatment infertility MOPP > ABVD; males > females sperm banking should be discussed premature menopause secondary malignancy skin, AML, lung, MDS, NHL, thyroid, breast... cardiac disease
--- Slide 45 ---
Late Complications of Hodgkin’s Disease Hypothyroidism after irradiation of the neck. Constrictive pericarditis after radiotherapy to the mediastinum. Infertility after use of alkylating agents. Heart failure after Adriamycin treatment.
--- Slide 46 ---
