slides.text: HODGKIN’S LYMPHOMA Dr Ademola Adewoyin lECTURER /consultant haematologist

HD: Definition Neoplastic disorder with development of specific infiltrate containing pathologic Reed-Sternberg (RS) cells. It usually arises in lymph nodes and spreads to contiguous groups. Extra-nodal presentation are rare. Disease is associated with defective cellular immunity .

Hodgkin’s Disease Background first described in 1832 by Dr. Thomas Hodgkin characterized by the presence of Reed-Sternberg cells multinucleated giant cells described by Sternberg in 1898 and Reed in 1902 classified as an infectious disease until 1950’s

Thomas Hodgkin (1798-1866) Thomas Hodgkin published in 1832 the first description of lymphoma, specifically of the form named after him, Hodgkin's lymphoma. Name Hodgkin's Disease proposed in 1865 by Wiks.

Characteristics of HD Usually arise in LNs, preferentially cervical region Majority manifest clinically in the young Neoplastic tissues usually contain a small number of scattered large mono-nucleated and multi-nucleated tumor cells designated Hodgkin and Reed- sternberge cells or HRS cells) The tumor cells are often ringed by T-lymphocytes in a rosette -like manner In contrast with NHL where there had been a steady increase in incidence, the absolute incidence of HD has not apparently changed.

HL: Histology Reed-Sternberg cells (or RS variants) in the affected tissues cell of origin: germinal centre B-cell most cells in affected lymph node are polyclonal reactive lymphoid cells, not neoplastic cells
Reed-Sternberg cell
Epidemiology
Hodgkin’s Disease: Epidemiology 14% of malignant lymphomas 0.5% of all malignancies Highly treatable and curable even when disseminated.
Hodgkin’s Disease: Epidemiology men > women whites > blacks > Asians no clear risk factors, several implicated EBV (pathogen or passenger) HIV woodworking, farming rare familial aggregations

Epidemiology bimodal age distribution : 15-35 years and above 50 years male predominance M:F = 1.7:1 More common in affluent families with few siblings. In developing countries, more common in young children
Etiology

Etiology of Hodgkin’s Disease/ Associated (etiological?) factors Reed-Sternberg cells are the malignant cells. Minor population in the malignant tissues many normal lymphocytes, eosinophils, other cells Cell of origin is now known to be of B cell origin. Some R-S cells contain EBV genomes indicating EBV infection smaller family size higher socio-economic status caucasian > non- caucasian ?possible genetic predisposition other: HIV? occupation? herbicides?
A possible model of pathogenesis germinal centre B cell transforming event(s) loss of apoptosis RS cell inflammatory response EBV? cytokines
Reed-Sternberg Cell
Clinical Presentation .

Clinical Presentation Non-tender lymph nodes enlargement ( localised ) neck and supraclavicular area 60-80% mediastinal adenopathy 50% other ( abdominal, extranodal disease ) systemic symptoms (B symptoms) 30% unexplained fever unexplained night sweats unexplained weight loss (10% per 6 months) other symptoms fatigue, weakness, pruritus cough , chest pain, shortness of breath, vena cava syndrome abdominal pain, bowel disturbances, ascites bone pain

Other Signs and Symptoms Pel-Ebstein fever. relapsing, high-grade fever that can reach 105-106°F, periodicity of 7-10 days. Fever spikes abrupt in onset and resolution Pain on drinking alcohol. Pel-Ebstein Fever

Clinical Features T cell mediated immune deficiency, even in early stage disease. Prone to infections: Herpes zoster (“shingles”) in one fourth of patients Fungal or mycobacterial infections Immune defect may persist even after lymphoma is cured. Predictable contiguous spread of disease: cervical nodes to mediastinum or axilla mediastinum to para- otic nodes or spleen, etc. Basis for staging and treatment decisions.
Diagnosis .

Diagnosis Excisional biopsy of a lymph node. Fine needle aspirate is not sufficient to make the diagnosis of Hodgkin’s disease. Same as for non-Hodgkin’s: Hx + PE, labs, CT scans, bone marrow biopsy PLUS: Gallium scan Lymphangiogram or staging laparotomy can be done ONLY if results would affect treatment decisions
Diagnosis of Hodgkin Disease is based on microscopic examination of lymph node or other involved tissue it requires identification of diagnostic Reed-Sternberg cells
Classification

Classification Comprised of two disease entities Nodular Lymphocyte Predominant Hodgkin Lymphoma[NLPHD] Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma[CHL] They distinctly defer in their clinical features and behavior as well as the composition of their cellular background

Hodgkin Lymphoma Classification “Classic” Hodgkin’s Disease nodular sclerosis mixed cellularity lymphocyte depleted (very rare) classical lymphocyte rich HRS cells CD30 and CD15 positive nodular lymphocyte predominant HRS cells (L&H cells) have B cell markers CD 20 and surface Immunoglobulin

Hodgkin’s Disease Approach to the Patient staging evaluation Hx & PE CBC, diff, plts ESR, LDH, albumin, LFT’s, Cr CT scans chest/abd/pelvis bone marrow evaluation **PET or gallium scan** **lymphangiogram or laparotomy**
Subtypes of Hodgkin’s Disease NOTE Unlike non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, in Hodgkin’s Disease the histologic subtype does not determine how the disease is treated.

Staging Classification Ann Arbor modified by Cotswolds Stage I: involvement of single lymph node region or lymphoid structure Stage II: involvement of two or more lymph node regions on same side of diaphragm Stage III: involvement of lymph node regions or structures on both sides of diaphragm III 1 : with splenic hilar,celiac,portal nodes III 2 : with para-aortic,iliac,mesenteric nodes Stage IV: involvement of extranodal site(s) A. Asymptomatic B. Symptomatic (B symptoms) X. Bulky disease ( > 1/3 widening of mediastinum, > 10cm max.dimension of nodal mass) E. Involvement of a single, localised, extranodal site

Ann Arbor Staging System for Hodgkin's Disease and Non-Hodgkin's Lymphoma Stage I Stage II Stage III Stage IV Reprinted with permission. Adapted from Skarin. Dana-Farber Cancer Institute Atlas of Diagnostic Oncology . 1991.

Modified Ann Arbor Staging “E” designation for extranodal disease B symptoms recurrent drenching night sweats during previous month unexplained, persistent, or recurrent fever with temps above 38 C during the previous month unexplained weight loss of more than 10% of the body weight during the previous 6 months Criteria for bulk 10 cm nodal mass mediastinal mass > 1/3 thorax diameter

Staging evaluation for Hodgkin’s Disease (1) Essential pathologic documentation by hemopathologist physical examination documentation of B symptoms laboratory evaluation complete blood count, ESR liver function tests renal function tests lactate dehydrogenase chest radiograph ultrasonography CT scan of chest, abdomen and pelvis bone marrow aspiration / biopsy (bilateral)

Staging evaluation for Hodgkin’s Disease (2) Essential under certain circumstances liver biopsy gallium scan technetium bone scan bone radiographs MRI bipedal lymphangiogram staging laparotomy Useful but not essential tests cell-surface marker phenotypic analysis gene rearrangement analysis
Treatment .

Treatment of Hodgkin Disesae (1) With appropriate treatment about 85% of patients with Hodgkin disease are curable I A,B: Radiation therapy II A : combination chemotherapy + Radiotherapy IIB; IIIA, B; IV A,B : combination chemotherapy (+/- radiotherapy)
Treatment of Hodgkin Disesae (2) Radiation therapy mantle field paraaortic field pelvic field dose: 35-40 Gy/T Combination chemotherapy ABVD BEACOPP
Treatment and Prognosis Stage Treatment Failure-free survival Overall 5 year survival I,II ABVD x 4 & radiation 70-80% 80-90% III,IV ABVD x 6 60-70% 70-80%

Hodgkin Lymphoma Adverse prognostic features for stage I & II (EORTC data) more than 3 nodal sites bulky adenopathy ESR > 50 B symptoms invasion into critical organs male age > 40 MC or LD subtype should probably not receive XRT alone if any of the above present (excessive relapse rate)

Hodgkin Lymphoma Independent adverse prognostic factors advanced stage (III-IV) male sex age > 45 albumin < 4 gm/dl HgB < 10.5 mg/dl stage IV disease WBC count > 15,000/mm 3 lymphocyte count < 600/mm 3 (Hasenclever et al, NEJM 339,1506-1514;1998)
Hodgkin’s Disease Results of Treatment stage 5 year overall survival I 90% II 90% III 80% IV 65%

Chemotherapy Regimens MOPP M echlorethamine, O ncovin, P rocarbazine, P rednisone ABVD A driamycin, B leomycin, V inblastine, D acarbazine BEACOPP Bleomycin, Etoposide, Adriamycin, Cyclophos, Oncovin,Pred, Procarbacin

Treatment Options Often, patients who relapse after radiotherapy can be cured by salvage chemotherapy. Combined chemotherapy and radiotherapy is given for bulky mediastinal masses. Chemotherapy now being tested for earlier stages of the disease.

Late Complications of Hodgkin’s Disease High incidence of second malignancies leukemia first 10 years, solid tumors over time. Leukemia in patients receiving alkylating agents or combined chemo/XRT. Lung cancer and breast cancer in patients receiving XRT to chest. Lung cancer especially high in smokers.

Long term complications of treatment infertility MOPP > ABVD; males > females sperm banking should be discussed premature menopause secondary malignancy skin, AML, lung, MDS, NHL, thyroid, breast... cardiac disease

introduction Lymphomas are a heterogeneous group of clonal (neoplastic) diseases that share the single characteristic of arising as the result of a somatic mutation(s) in a lymphocyte progenitor. Lymphoma previously was referred to as reticulum cell sarcoma, lymphosarcoma, giant follicular lymphoma. The malignant cells arise mainly from B- or T-cell lineage, and a few are derived from NK cells.
--- Slide 4 ---
INTRODUCTION - II Of the lymphomas, Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma account for 85% of the cases while Hodgkin’s Lymphoma accounts for15%. In Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma, any site of the lymphatic system can be the primary site of origin of the disorder, including lymph nodes, gut-associated lymphatic tissue, skin, or spleen. Any organ, such as the thyroid, lung, bone, brain, or gonads, can be involved either by spread from lymphatic sites or as a manifestation of primary extra-nodal disease.
--- Slide 5 ---
INTRODUCTION - III It is the fifth most common cancer in the USA and Australia, and the most commonly occurring blood cancer with about 4000-5000 cases diagnosed yearly. Since the early 1970’s, the incidence rates for Non- Hodgkin”s lymphoma have nearly doubled. An increased incidence of malignant lymphomas has been associated with HIV/AIDS pandemic, with predilection for extranodal sites including the central nervous system (CNS).
--- Slide 6 ---
Relative frequency of lymphoid malignancies Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma-62.4% Plasma cell disorders-16% CLL-9% ALL-3.8% Hodgkin’s Lymphoma-8.2%

Farming has been a constant association with higher lymphoma incidence, although other occupations have been identified. Lymphoma is slightly common in males than females and in Americans of European descent than in Americans of African descent (i.e. commoner in white than in blacks). Generally The male female ratio is about 1.7:1 Burkitt lymphoma (BL) occurs most frequently in tropical Africa, whereas T cell leukemia/lymphoma is most common in southwest Japan and the Caribbean basin.

The average annual adjusted mortality rate is approximately 400 to 500 deaths per year Childhood lymphomas differ significantly from adult disease in clinical presentation and prognosis. Localised disease and indolent lymphomas are rare in children. Most lymphomas in children are of aggressive histology.

introduction Lymphomas are a heterogeneous group of clonal (neoplastic) diseases that share the single characteristic of arising as the result of a somatic mutation(s) in a lymphocyte progenitor. Lymphoma previously was referred to as reticulum cell sarcoma, lymphosarcoma, giant follicular lymphoma. The malignant cells arise mainly from B- or T-cell lineage, and a few are derived from NK cells.

INTRODUCTION - II Of the lymphomas, Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma account for 85% of the cases while Hodgkin’s Lymphoma accounts for15%. In Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma, any site of the lymphatic system can be the primary site of origin of the disorder, including lymph nodes, gut-associated lymphatic tissue, skin, or spleen. Any organ, such as the thyroid, lung, bone, brain, or gonads, can be involved either by spread from lymphatic sites or as a manifestation of primary extra-nodal disease.

INTRODUCTION - III It is the fifth most common cancer in the USA and Australia, and the most commonly occurring blood cancer with about 4000-5000 cases diagnosed yearly. Since the early 1970’s, the incidence rates for Non- Hodgkin”s lymphoma have nearly doubled. An increased incidence of malignant lymphomas has been associated with HIV/AIDS pandemic, with predilection for extranodal sites including the central nervous system (CNS).
Relative frequency of lymphoid malignancies Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma-62.4% Plasma cell disorders-16% CLL-9% ALL-3.8% Hodgkin’s Lymphoma-8.2%

Farming has been a constant association with higher lymphoma incidence, although other occupations have been identified. Lymphoma is slightly common in males than females and in Americans of European descent than in Americans of African descent (i.e. commoner in white than in blacks). Generally The male female ratio is about 1.7:1 Burkitt lymphoma (BL) occurs most frequently in tropical Africa, whereas T cell leukemia/lymphoma is most common in southwest Japan and the Caribbean basin.

The incidence of lymphomas increases with age and peaks at the seventh decade of life., Median Age at presentation= 50 years (52+/-0.5 years in a study done in Ubth by Omoti et al). The average annual adjusted mortality rate is approximately 400 to 500 deaths per year Childhood lymphomas differ significantly from adult disease in clinical presentation and prognosis. Localised disease and indolent lymphomas are rare in children. Most lymphomas in children are of aggressive histology.

aeTIOPATHOGENESIS THE exact cause has been unidentified in the large majority of cases but a few cases are known to play a role in lymphomagenesis : EXPOSURE TO CHEMICAL AGENTS like organochlorines, organophosphates, and phenoxyacid herbicides EXPOSURE TO RADIATION survivors of the atomic bombing in Hiroshima, individuals radiated for ankylosing spondylitis patients and with Hodgkin lymphoma who were treated with radiation therapy). CLINICAL presentation Constitutional symptoms (unexplained fever of 38°C or higher, night sweats, pruritus and loss of more than 10% of body weight in 6 months). Widespread painless lymphadenopathy, spread is not usually contiguous. Superior vena cava syndrome due to a mediasternal mass. Jaw swelling (African Burkitt’s lymphoma). Skin plaques or nodules (Mycosis fungoides).

CLINICAL PRESENTATION - II Features suggestive of bone marrow suppression. Jaundice(5-10% of cases). Hepatosplenomegaly. Symptoms and signs may be due to the involvement of particular organs ( extranodal disease) (e.g. Skin, gastrointestinal tract, salivary glands, lungs, renal tract and central nervous system). Metabolic complications (with features of hyperuricemia, hypercalcemia, and renal failure.
ANN-ARBOR STAGING(1965/66)

INVESTIGATIONS Histological diagnosis from biopsy of a lymph node, bone marrow or extranodal mass is essential PBF ( shows normochromoia , normocytes, leucoerythroblastic pix(if there’s extensive BM infiltration), pancytopenia, lymphoma cells) Immunophenotyping Cytogenetic and immunoglobulin or TCR rearrangement analysis, as well as, more recently, DNA microarray testing.

Other investigations Complete blood count. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Chemistry studies reflecting major organ function. Coomb’s test. Investigations for staging---CXR, CT scan, MRI, PET scan or Gallium scam

Other investigations Viral studies. Lumbar Puncture. Serum levels of Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH) and β2- macroglobulin. Serum Protein Electrophoresis ( seen in approx. 20% of patients with SLL or FL). Serum Uric acid. Serum Calcium.

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS Castleman disease , which can present lymphadenopathy, +/-systemic symptoms, anaemia and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia , and the condition has been associated with overproduction of interleukin 6, possibly produced by human herpesvirus 8. Sinus histiocytosis with massive lymphadenopathy (Rosai-Dorfman’s disease) usually presents with bulky lymphadenopathy in children or young adults. The disease is usually non-progressive and self-limited, but patients can manifest autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Hodgkin’s lymphoma.

Lymphomatoid papulosis is a cutaneous lymphoproliferative disorder that is often confused with anaplastic large cell lymphoma involving the skin. The cells of lymphomatoid papulosis are similar to those seen in lymphoma and stain for CD30, and T cell receptor gene rearrangements are sometimes seen. However, the condition is characterized by waxing and waning skin lesions that usually heal, leaving small scars. Other causes of generalized lymphadenopathy

Adverse Prognostic Factors in NHL Age > 60 years at presentation. Presence of constitutional “B” symptoms. Elevated serum LDH . Elevated beta2 microglobulin . High proliferative rate based on ki-67 value. Poor performance status at diagnosis (>1 (ECOG).

Prognostic factors Stage III or IV disease. P53 mutations. Bcl-2 expression poor risk in DLBCL (not with R-CHOP treatment) [ Bcl-6 expression favourable in dlbcl (not with R-CHOP treatment)]. T-cell phenotype. Bulky tumour (diameter > 10cm ).

MANAGEMENT Supportive Definitive- Chemotherapy / Radiotherapy / Biological therapy / Bone marrow stem cell transplantation. N.B: Treatment generally depends on the severity of the disease i.e. whether indolent-,aggressive or highly aggressive.
SUPPORTIVE MANAGEMENT Use of CVC lines. Antimicrobial cover. Blood product support. Use of haemopoietic growth factors. Counselling. Psychotherapy. Prevention of tumour lysis syndrome.

DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT - INDOLENT DISEASE Watchful waiting in asymptomatic patients; treatment indicated in the presence of large tumour load: Symptomatic advanced disease (stage III/IV) Constitutional (B) symptoms Pressure effects on vital structures, such as the CNS Tumour-related myelosuppression . In 40-60% of cases, indolent B-cell tumours may transform to aggressive phenotypes , whether treated or not.

Combination therapy is mandatory. Radiotherapy is given to relieve bulky disease and/or large extranodal disease. CHOP is the gold standard for b oth B-and T-cell aggressive NHLs.

--- Slide 1 ---
Paraproteinaemias Prof. OLOWOSELU,F O
--- Slide 2 ---
Learning objectives Define paraproteinemia and understand M-protein physiology Recognize causes of paraproteinemia Understand the pathogenesis and diagnosis of multiple myeloma Interpret laboratory findings Outline clinical management strategies
--- Slide 3 ---
Paraprotein Im munoglobulin produced from a single clone of plasma cells ( monoclonal antibody or M protein ) is called a p araprotein . ("M"for monoclonal) . Paraprotein in excessive amount in the plasma is referred to as paraproteinaemia Paraproteinaemias are usually as a result of clonal transformation of B-cells which retain their ability to mature into plasma cells
--- Slide 4 ---
Paraproteinaemias Are heterogeneous group of disorders character ized by abnormal proliferation of a single clone of plasma cells or B lymphocytes, associated with the presence of excessive accumulation of monoclonal I mmunoglobulin or its fragments in the serum and/or urine.
--- Slide 5 ---
Paraproteinaemias Paraproteinemias may be categorized according to the type of monoclonal protein found in blood: 1. Light chains only (or Bence Jones protein). This may be associated with multiple myeloma or AL amyloidosis ; 2. Heavy chains only (also known as "heavy chain disease"); 3. Whole immunoglobulins- "M-protein".
--- Slide 6 ---
Classification of Para proteinaemias Malignant monoclonal gammopathies Multiple myeloma ( IgG , IgA , IgD , IgE and free light chain) Smoldering multiple myeloma Plasma cell leukaemia Nonsecretory myeloma Osteosclerotic myeloma (POEMS Syndrome) Plasmacytoma Solitary plasmacytoma of bone/ extramedullary plasmacytoma Monoclonal gammopathies of undetermined significance Waldenstrom’s macroglobulinemia Heavy chain diseases ( γ - HCD , α - HCD , µ- HCD ) Primary Amyloidosis
--- Slide 7 ---
Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined signiﬁcance (MGUS) The following criteria must be met: Serum monoclonal protein <3 g/ dL Clonal bone marrow plasma cells <10% Absence of end-organ damage such as hypercalcemia , renal insufﬁciency , anemia, and bone lesions (CRAB)
--- Slide 8 ---
Smoldering multiple myeloma (also referred to as asymptomatic multiple myeloma) The following criteria must be met: Serum monoclonal protein ( IgG or IgA ) 3 g/ dL and/or clonal bone marrow plasma cells 10% Absence of end-organ damage such as lytic bone lesions, anemia, hypercalcemia , or renal failure
--- Slide 9 ---
Spectrum of Paraproteinemia MGUS: <10% plasma cells, <3 g/dL M-protein, no CRAB features Smoldering MM: ≥10% plasma cells or ≥3 g/dL M-protein, no CRAB Multiple Myeloma: ≥10% plasma cells, CRAB features present Others: WM, AL Amyloidosis
--- Slide 10 ---
Multiple myeloma is a neoplastic plasma-cell disorder that is characterized by clonal proliferation of malignant plasma cells in the bone marrow, overproduction of monoclonal protein in the blood or urine, and associated organ dysfunction. It is the most common and important monoclonal gammopathy and usually presents as multiple tumour masses throughout the skeletal system. Multiple Myeloma
--- Slide 11 ---
Epidemiology It accounts for 10% of all haematological malignancies and 1% of all cancers. The incidence is higher among blacks . Median age at diagnosis is 67 years. There is a slight male predominance .
--- Slide 12 ---
Etiologic factors The aetiology of multiple myeloma is unknown and several associated risk factors include: Occupational factor (prolonged low-grade radiation exposure of those living near nuclear facilities and workers in agriculture, metal, rubber, wood, leather, paint and petroleum industries). Environmental factor
--- Slide 13 ---
Etiologic factors Chronic antigenic stimulation (repeated infections, allergic conditions, autoimmune diseases e.g Human herpes virus 8 and hepatitis C are aetiological pathogens in multiple myeloma). Frequent chromosomal abnormalities and several other genetic mutations contribute to the development and/or progression of MM. del17p and translocations t(11:14)(q13:q32), and t(4:14) are most common Monoclonal Gammopathies of Undetermined Significance (MGUS)
--- Slide 14 ---
Pathogenesis Three primary processes lead to the complex disruption of organs in multiple myeloma: Plasma cell expansion in BM Overproduction of monoclonal immunoglobulin Overproduction of various cytokines
--- Slide 15 ---
Plasma cell expansion in BM Plasma cell establishes a malignant clone. Normal BM is gradually replaced by the slowly expanding malignant clone. Decrease in the number of normal blood cells leads to pancytopenia . Pancytopenia occurs after sequence of anemia, thrombocytopenia and neutropenia . Expanding plasmacytoma in the BM frequently cause bone surface “cortex” destruction.

Paraprotein Im munoglobulin produced from a single clone of plasma cells ( monoclonal antibody or M protein ) is called a p araprotein . ("M"for monoclonal) . Paraprotein in excessive amount in the plasma is referred to as paraproteinaemia Paraproteinaemias are usually as a result of clonal transformation of B-cells which retain their ability to mature into plasma cells

Paraproteinaemias Are heterogeneous group of disorders character ized by abnormal proliferation of a single clone of plasma cells or B lymphocytes, associated with the presence of excessive accumulation of monoclonal I mmunoglobulin or its fragments in the serum and/or urine.

Paraproteinaemias Paraproteinemias may be categorized according to the type of monoclonal protein found in blood: 1. Light chains only (or Bence Jones protein). This may be associated with multiple myeloma or AL amyloidosis ; 2. Heavy chains only (also known as "heavy chain disease"); 3. Whole immunoglobulins- "M-protein".

Smoldering multiple myeloma (also referred to as asymptomatic multiple myeloma) The following criteria must be met: Serum monoclonal protein ( IgG or IgA ) 3 g/ dL and/or clonal bone marrow plasma cells 10% Absence of end-organ damage such as lytic bone lesions, anemia, hypercalcemia , or renal failure

Multiple myeloma is a neoplastic plasma-cell disorder that is characterized by clonal proliferation of malignant plasma cells in the bone marrow, overproduction of monoclonal protein in the blood or urine, and associated organ dysfunction. It is the most common and important monoclonal gammopathy and usually presents as multiple tumour masses throughout the skeletal system. Multiple Myeloma

Epidemiology It accounts for 10% of all haematological malignancies and 1% of all cancers. The incidence is higher among blacks . Median age at diagnosis is 67 years. There is a slight male predominance .

Etiologic factors The aetiology of multiple myeloma is unknown and several associated risk factors include: Occupational factor (prolonged low-grade radiation exposure of those living near nuclear facilities and workers in agriculture, metal, rubber, wood, leather, paint and petroleum industries). Environmental factor

Etiologic factors Chronic antigenic stimulation (repeated infections, allergic conditions, autoimmune diseases e.g Human herpes virus 8 and hepatitis C are aetiological pathogens in multiple myeloma). Frequent chromosomal abnormalities and several other genetic mutations contribute to the development and/or progression of MM. del17p and translocations t(11:14)(q13:q32), and t(4:14) are most common Monoclonal Gammopathies of Undetermined Significance (MGUS)

--- Slide 1 ---
MYELOPROLIFERTIVE DISORDERS Dr. OLOWOSELU , F. O.
--- Slide 2 ---
INTRODUCTION These are clonal neoplastic disorders of pluripotent haematopoietic stem cell (HSC) characterized by excessive proliferation of one or more of the myeloid cell lineages ( granulocytic, erythroid,megakaryocytic , and mast cells) Myeloproliferative disorders: 1. Originates from a single stem cell. 2.one cell line predominates in a given disorder. 3. Enlargements of spleen and liver occur commonly. 4. Usually in adults with a peak in the 5 th to 7 th decade
--- Slide 3 ---
INTRODUCTION 4 Maturation of blood cells is relatively normal, leading to increased numbers of mature red cells, platelets, or granulocytes in the absence of a physiological stimulus. • There is a close relationship among different MPNs with potential for: - Interconversion between subtypes - Overlapping clinical and pathological features - Progression to myelofibrosis or acute leukemia • Extramedullary hematopoiesis : - Blood cell production occurs outside the bone marrow - Commonly results in hepatomegaly and splenomegaly
--- Slide 4 ---
THE HEMATOPOIETIC TREE
--- Slide 5 ---
CLASSIFICATION Based on nature of predominant proliferating cell line: Primary polycythemia ( erythroid ) Essential thrombocythemia (megakaryocytic) Chronic myeloid leukemia (granulocytes) Primary myelofibrosis (fibrous tissue) Chronic neutrophilic leukaemia Chronic eosinophilic leukaemia Mastocytosis Myeloproliferative neoplasm (unclassifiable)
--- Slide 6 ---
PATHOGENESIS The presence of mutated, constitutively activated tyrosine kinases protein: JAK2 . Tyrosine kinases activation normally occurs by the binding of hematopoietic growth factors to surface receptors on the marrow progenitor cells.
--- Slide 7 ---
PATHOGENESIS Mutated constitutively activated tyrosine kinases results in the growth factor-independent proliferation and survival of marrow progenitors Proliferation of HSCs leads to a hypercellular marrow. Proliferating cells undergo normal differentiation, which results in increased blood counts of one or more mature blood elements.
--- Slide 8 ---
POLYCYTHAEMIA
--- Slide 9 ---
Definition and Classification Polycythemia (Erythrocytosis) is defined as an increase in the total red cell mass (RCM), usually with a corresponding increase in haemoglobin level. The increase in RCM can be: • Absolute – where red cell mass is actually increased - Primary Polycythemia : e.g., Polycythemia Vera (PV) - Secondary Polycythemia : due to increased EPO • Relative ( Pseudopolycythemia ) – red cell mass is normal but plasma volume is reduced
--- Slide 10 ---
Suspicion and Diagnostic Thresholds Polycythemia is suspected by finding a raised haematocrit (HCT): • In men: - Haemoglobin (Hb) > 18.5 g/dL - Haematocrit (HCT) > 0.52 • In women: - Haemoglobin (Hb) > 16.5 g/dL - Haematocrit (HCT) > 0.48
--- Slide 11 ---
Relative Polycythemia Characterized by reduced plasma volume with a normal red cell mass. May result from dehydration: following vomiting, diarrhea , excessive use of diurectics It can occur in Gaisbock syndrome( spurious polycythemia ) Middle age Overweight Hypertensive anxiety
--- Slide 12 ---
POLYCYTHAEMIA {2D5ABB26-0587-4C30-8999-92F81FD0307C} Causes of absolute polycythemia Primary Polycythemia ( rubra ) vera Secondary Caused by physiologically appropriate erythropoietin increase in : High altitudes Pulmonary disease and alveolar hypoventilation (sleep apnea) Cardiovascular disease , especially cyanotic heart disease Increased affinity haemoglobin Familial (congenital) polycythemia Heavy cigarette smoking Caused by inappropriate erythropoietin increase in : Renal cancer Tumors such as uterine, renal cell, hepatocellular carcinoma Causes of relative polycythemia Haemoconcentration (dehydration due to diarrhoea and vomiting). Gaisbock syndrome (spurious polycythaemia ).
--- Slide 13 ---
Causes of Absolute Polycythemia – Secondary Caused by physiologically appropriate erythropoietin increase: • High altitudes • Pulmonary disease and alveolar hypoventilation (e.g., sleep apnea ) • Cardiovascular disease, especially cyanotic heart disease • Increased affinity haemoglobin / Familial (congenital) polycythemia • Heavy cigarette smoking Caused by inappropriate erythropoietin increase: • Renal cell carcinoma • Tumors such as uterine, renal, and hepatocellular carcinoma
--- Slide 14 ---
Causes of Relative Polycythemia Relative polycythemia occurs when plasma volume is reduced: • Haemoconcentration due to dehydration (e.g., diarrhoea, vomiting) • Gaisbock syndrome (stress polycythemia or spurious polycythemia )
--- Slide 15 ---
POLYCYTHEMIA VERA(PCV) • A myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by clonal proliferation of erythroid, granulocytic, and megakaryocytic lineages. • Caused by JAK2 V617F mutation in ~95% of cases. • Leads to autonomous red cell production, independent of erythropoietin.
--- Slide 16 ---
POLYCYTHEMIA VERA Two phases of PV can be recognized: A proliferative or polycythemic phase (initial phase characterized by proliferation of erythoid cells leading to increased red cell mass). A “ spent”, or post- polycythemic phase (this is characterized by cytopaenia and myelofibrosis ).
--- Slide 17 ---
Epidemiology PCV is the most common myeloproliferative disorder. The incidence is approximately 3 cases per 100000 per year. Median age at diagnosis is 60 years (NB: PCV occurs at all ages but it is very rare below 30 years).
--- Slide 18 ---
Pathophysiology No obvious etiology exists. A genetic predisposition has been reported in some families. An increased number of cases have been reported in survivors of the Hiroshima atomic bomb. Cytogenetic abnormalities are found in only 10-20% of patients at diagnosis. JAK2 V617F mutation associated Growth factor- independent proliferation and progenitor survival
--- Slide 20 ---
Pathophysiology Increased red cell production in PV results in an increased red cell mass and increased blood viscosity which can lead to vascular thrombosis and/or bleeding. The hematocrit is directly proportional to the number of thrombotic events. Studies have demonstrated a reduction in cerebral blood flow in patients with hematocrits above 53%. Thrombocytosis can also contribute to bleeding and thrombosis.
--- Slide 21 ---
Clinical Features Patients are frequently asymptomatic at diagnosis and are discovered incidentally when an elevated hematocrit is noted on a FBC . Most patients will develop symptoms as the hematocrit and/or platelet count increase.
--- Slide 22 ---
PV Clinical Features Major symptoms can be listed as follows: Symptoms of hyperviscosity associated with an elevated hematocrit include headache, blurred vision, dizziness, weakness, priapism and paresthesias . Pruritus typically following a hot shower may be the main complaint. The etiology is unclear but may be associated with cutaneous mast cell degranulation.
--- Slide 23 ---
PV Clinical Features Venous or arterial thrombosis, involving small and large vessels is common. Complications include cyanosis, TIA, CVA , myocardial infarction, and deep vein thrombosis. Unusual sites of thromboses are seen more frequently in PV: splenic , hepatic, portal, and mesenteric veins . Ten percent of patients with Budd- Chiari syndrome (hepatic/ IVC thrombosis) have coexisting PV. Abnormalities in platelet function can lead to epistaxis , bruising, gastrointestinal and gingival bleeding.
--- Slide 24 ---
PV Clinical Features 8 Hyper metabolism caused by increased blood cell turnover can lead to hyperuricemia and gout. 9 Gastrointestinal complaints are common including epigastric discomfort and peptic ulcer disease. Physical findings include splenomegaly , hepatomegaly and facial plethora.
--- Slide 25 ---
Full blood count : 1. The haemoglobin , haematocrit and red cell count are increased (In men, Hb >18.5 g/ dL or HCT >0.52 and in women, Hb >16.5 g/ dL or HCT >0.48). 2. leukocytosis, raised platelets and raised basophil count is present in about half of the patients. JAK2 mutation analysis: JAK2 mutation is present in the bone marrow and peripheral blood granulocytes in 95% of patients. Laboratory findings
--- Slide 26 ---
Neutrophil alkaline phosphatase (NAP) score is usually increased. Bone marrow examination: The bone marrow is hypercellular with prominent megakaryocytes , best assessed by a trephine biopsy. Serum erythropoietin assay: Serum erythropoietin usually low in polycythemia vera but high in secondary polycythemia . Arterial oxygen saturation Laboratory findings (Cont.)
--- Slide 27 ---
Category A ( major ) Category B ( minor ) Elevated red cell mass ( In men, Hb >18.5 g/ dL or HCT >0.52 and in women, Hb >16.5 g/ dL or HCT >0.48). JAK2-V617F mutation Hypercellular bone marrow Low erythropoietin ( EPO ) EEC growth in vitro Criteria for diagnosis of polycythaemia ( rubra ) vera Diagnosis of PV requires that the patient meets both major criteria plus one minor criterion or the first major criterion and two minor criteria.
--- Slide 28 ---
PV Treatment Treatment focuses on decreasing the hematocrit to reduce plasma viscosity and its attendant complications. The goal of therapy is a hematocrit <45% and a platelet count < 400,000. Therapeutic options include: Phlebotomy In a newly diagnosed patient, phlebotomy (450mL) should be made two or three times weekly until the haematocrit is in the range of 40-45%, then as necessary to maintain haematocrit within this range Myelosuppressive agents such as Hydroxyurea , radioactive phosphorus and busulfan . Alpha interferon is also an option. - A small daily dose of aspirin is recommended for its anti-platelet effect. - Allopurinol to prevent urate nephropathy
--- Slide 29 ---
Prognosis Without therapy, median survival of patients with PV is only 6-18 months, but is more than 10 years with treatment. Major causes of death are thrombosis and hemorrhage. Up to 20% of patients develop acute myelogeneous leukemia or myelodysplastic syndrome which are fatal. PV patients can develop a “spent phase” late in their courses that resembles chronic idiopathic myelofibrosis with cytopenia and marrow hypoplasia and fibrosis – referred to as post polycythemic myelofibrosis or secondary myelofibrosis . Post polycythemic myelofibrosis frequently transforms to acute leukemia.
--- Slide 30 ---
THANK YOU FOR LISTENING
--- Slide 31 ---
ESSENTIAL THROMBOCYTHEMIA (ET) Clonal myeloproliferative disorder that involves primarily the megakaryocyte cell line. It leads to the dysregulated production of large numbers of mature megakaryocytes in the marrow resulting in marked rise in platelet counts. The etiology of ET is unknown. JAK2 mutation are found in approximately 50% of patients with ET.
--- Slide 32 ---
ET Epidemiology The incidence of the disease is 2-3/100,000 individuals annually. Usually occurs at the age of 50-60 years. A second peak occurs at approximately 30 years of age, typically in women.
--- Slide 33 ---
ET Clinical features Many patients are asymptomatic and discovered when a routine blood count is performed. Bleeding manifestation and a predisposition to thrombotic events are the main clinical findings Thrombotic events include strokes, TIA, retinal artery or venous occlusions, coronary artery ischemia, pulmonary embolism, hepatic or portal vein thrombosis, DVT and digital ischemia.
--- Slide 34 ---
ET Clinical features Erythromelalgia is classic of ET and is believed to be due to microvascular thrombosis of the digital vessel of fingers and toes. Spontaneous abortion due to placental thrombosis. Bleeding occurs most commonly from mucosal surfaces especially the gastrointestinal tract. There may be mild splenomegaly and less often hepatomegaly .
--- Slide 35 ---
ET Clinical features Transformation of ET to acute myeloid leukemia or a myelodysplastic syndrome occurs in fewer than 5% of patients. There can also be delayed disease transformation into a fibrotic state called post thrombocythemia myeloid metaplasia or myelofibrosis
--- Slide 36 ---
ET Lab features Peripheral blood film shows marked thrombocytosis . The platelets often display anisocytosis (range from tiny forms to giant platelets). The white blood cell count and differential are usually normal. The red blood cells are normocytic and normochromic. Leukoerythroblastosis . The bone marrow biopsy is usually hypercellular . The most striking abnormality is marked proliferation of large and giant megakaryocytes , usually occurring in loose clusters.
--- Slide 37 ---
Diagnostic Criteria for ET 1. Persistent elevation of the platelet count ≥450 x 10 9 /L. 2. Megakaryocyte proliferation with large and mature morphology: little or no granulocyte or erythroid proliferation. 3. Not meeting WHO criteria for CML , PV, PMF , MDS, or other myeloid neoplasm. 4. Demonstration of JAK2-V617F or other clonal marker or in the absence of a clonal marker, no evidence of reactive thrombocytosis .
--- Slide 38 ---
ET Treatment and Prognosis ET is an indolent disorder, characterised by long symptom free intervals, interrupted by occasional life-threatening thromboembolic or hemorrhagic episodes. Most patients enjoy a normal life expectancy. Risk stratification in ET is primarily based upon factors that influence the occurrence of thrombotic complications. Patients are considered to be at high risk if they are > 60 years of age and/or have a prior history of thrombosis.
--- Slide 39 ---
ET Treatment and Prognosis Therapeutic options include: Low dose Acetyl salicylic acid as an antiplatelet agent (e.g. effective in erythromelalgia ), Hydroxyurea (inhibits platelet production), Anagrelide (inhibits platelet aggregation and has a platelet lowering effect), Alpha Interferon and Radiophosphorous .
--- Slide 40 ---
THANK YOU
--- Slide 41 ---
PRIMARY MYELOFIBROSIS ( PMF ) Clonal disorder of pluripotent stem cell characterised by the proliferation of mainly megakaryocytic and granulocytic elements in the bone marrow associated with reactive deposition of bone marrow connective tissue. As the bone marrow becomes fibrotic and normal hematopoiesis can no longer occur, extramedullary hematopoiesis (EMH) occurs in the liver and spleen - splenomegaly and hepatomegaly which worsens throughout the disease course.
--- Slide 42 ---
PRIMARY MYELOFIBROSIS ( PMF ) The EMH seems to be ineffective and the patients become pancytopenic . slides.text: MYELOPROLIFERTIVE DISORDERS Dr. OLOWOSELU , F. O.

INTRODUCTION These are clonal neoplastic disorders of pluripotent haematopoietic stem cell (HSC) characterized by excessive proliferation of one or more of the myeloid cell lineages ( granulocytic, erythroid,megakaryocytic , and mast cells) Myeloproliferative disorders: 1. Originates from a single stem cell. 2.one cell line predominates in a given disorder. 3. Enlargements of spleen and liver occur commonly. 4. Usually in adults with a peak in the 5 th to 7 th decade

INTRODUCTION 4 Maturation of blood cells is relatively normal, leading to increased numbers of mature red cells, platelets, or granulocytes in the absence of a physiological stimulus. • There is a close relationship among different MPNs with potential for: - Interconversion between subtypes - Overlapping clinical and pathological features - Progression to myelofibrosis or acute leukemia • Extramedullary hematopoiesis : - Blood cell production occurs outside the bone marrow - Commonly results in hepatomegaly and splenomegaly
THE HEMATOPOIETIC TREE

CLASSIFICATION Based on nature of predominant proliferating cell line: Primary polycythemia ( erythroid ) Essential thrombocythemia (megakaryocytic) Chronic myeloid leukemia (granulocytes) Primary myelofibrosis (fibrous tissue) Chronic neutrophilic leukaemia Chronic eosinophilic leukaemia Mastocytosis Myeloproliferative neoplasm (unclassifiable)

PATHOGENESIS The presence of mutated, constitutively activated tyrosine kinases protein: JAK2 . Tyrosine kinases activation normally occurs by the binding of hematopoietic growth factors to surface receptors on the marrow progenitor cells.

PATHOGENESIS Mutated constitutively activated tyrosine kinases results in the growth factor-independent proliferation and survival of marrow progenitors Proliferation of HSCs leads to a hypercellular marrow. Proliferating cells undergo normal differentiation, which results in increased blood counts of one or more mature blood elements.
POLYCYTHAEMIA

Definition and Classification Polycythemia (Erythrocytosis) is defined as an increase in the total red cell mass (RCM), usually with a corresponding increase in haemoglobin level. The increase in RCM can be: • Absolute – where red cell mass is actually increased - Primary Polycythemia : e.g., Polycythemia Vera (PV) - Secondary Polycythemia : due to increased EPO • Relative ( Pseudopolycythemia ) – red cell mass is normal but plasma volume is reduced

Suspicion and Diagnostic Thresholds Polycythemia is suspected by finding a raised haematocrit (HCT): • In men: - Haemoglobin (Hb) > 18.5 g/dL - Haematocrit (HCT) > 0.52 • In women: - Haemoglobin (Hb) > 16.5 g/dL - Haematocrit (HCT) > 0.48

Relative Polycythemia Characterized by reduced plasma volume with a normal red cell mass. May result from dehydration: following vomiting, diarrhea , excessive use of diurectics It can occur in Gaisbock syndrome( spurious polycythemia ) Middle age Overweight Hypertensive anxiety

POLYCYTHAEMIA {2D5ABB26-0587-4C30-8999-92F81FD0307C} Causes of absolute polycythemia Primary Polycythemia ( rubra ) vera Secondary Caused by physiologically appropriate erythropoietin increase in : High altitudes Pulmonary disease and alveolar hypoventilation (sleep apnea) Cardiovascular disease , especially cyanotic heart disease Increased affinity haemoglobin Familial (congenital) polycythemia Heavy cigarette smoking Caused by inappropriate erythropoietin increase in : Renal cancer Tumors such as uterine, renal cell, hepatocellular carcinoma Causes of relative polycythemia Haemoconcentration (dehydration due to diarrhoea and vomiting). Gaisbock syndrome (spurious polycythaemia ).

Causes of Absolute Polycythemia – Secondary Caused by physiologically appropriate erythropoietin increase: • High altitudes • Pulmonary disease and alveolar hypoventilation (e.g., sleep apnea ) • Cardiovascular disease, especially cyanotic heart disease • Increased affinity haemoglobin / Familial (congenital) polycythemia • Heavy cigarette smoking Caused by inappropriate erythropoietin increase: • Renal cell carcinoma • Tumors such as uterine, renal, and hepatocellular carcinoma

Causes of Relative Polycythemia Relative polycythemia occurs when plasma volume is reduced: • Haemoconcentration due to dehydration (e.g., diarrhoea, vomiting) • Gaisbock syndrome (stress polycythemia or spurious polycythemia )

POLYCYTHEMIA VERA(PCV) • A myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by clonal proliferation of erythroid, granulocytic, and megakaryocytic lineages. • Caused by JAK2 V617F mutation in ~95% of cases. • Leads to autonomous red cell production, independent of erythropoietin.

POLYCYTHEMIA VERA Two phases of PV can be recognized: A proliferative or polycythemic phase (initial phase characterized by proliferation of erythoid cells leading to increased red cell mass). A “ spent”, or post- polycythemic phase (this is characterized by cytopaenia and myelofibrosis ).

Epidemiology PCV is the most common myeloproliferative disorder. The incidence is approximately 3 cases per 100000 per year. Median age at diagnosis is 60 years (NB: PCV occurs at all ages but it is very rare below 30 years).

Pathophysiology No obvious etiology exists. A genetic predisposition has been reported in some families. An increased number of cases have been reported in survivors of the Hiroshima atomic bomb. Cytogenetic abnormalities are found in only 10-20% of patients at diagnosis. JAK2 V617F mutation associated Growth factor- independent proliferation and progenitor survival

Pathophysiology Increased red cell production in PV results in an increased red cell mass and increased blood viscosity which can lead to vascular thrombosis and/or bleeding. The hematocrit is directly proportional to the number of thrombotic events. Studies have demonstrated a reduction in cerebral blood flow in patients with hematocrits above 53%. Thrombocytosis can also contribute to bleeding and thrombosis.

Clinical Features Patients are frequently asymptomatic at diagnosis and are discovered incidentally when an elevated hematocrit is noted on a FBC . Most patients will develop symptoms as the hematocrit and/or platelet count increase.

PV Clinical Features Major symptoms can be listed as follows: Symptoms of hyperviscosity associated with an elevated hematocrit include headache, blurred vision, dizziness, weakness, priapism and paresthesias . Pruritus typically following a hot shower may be the main complaint. The etiology is unclear but may be associated with cutaneous mast cell degranulation.

PV Clinical Features Venous or arterial thrombosis, involving small and large vessels is common. Complications include cyanosis, TIA, CVA , myocardial infarction, and deep vein thrombosis. Unusual sites of thromboses are seen more frequently in PV: splenic , hepatic, portal, and mesenteric veins . Ten percent of patients with Budd- Chiari syndrome (hepatic/ IVC thrombosis) have coexisting PV. Abnormalities in platelet function can lead to epistaxis , bruising, gastrointestinal and gingival bleeding.

PV Clinical Features 8 Hyper metabolism caused by increased blood cell turnover can lead to hyperuricemia and gout. 9 Gastrointestinal complaints are common including epigastric discomfort and peptic ulcer disease. Physical findings include splenomegaly , hepatomegaly and facial plethora.

Full blood count : 1. The haemoglobin , haematocrit and red cell count are increased (In men, Hb >18.5 g/ dL or HCT >0.52 and in women, Hb >16.5 g/ dL or HCT >0.48). 2. leukocytosis, raised platelets and raised basophil count is present in about half of the patients. JAK2 mutation analysis: JAK2 mutation is present in the bone marrow and peripheral blood granulocytes in 95% of patients. Laboratory findings

Neutrophil alkaline phosphatase (NAP) score is usually increased. Bone marrow examination: The bone marrow is hypercellular with prominent megakaryocytes , best assessed by a trephine biopsy. Serum erythropoietin assay: Serum erythropoietin usually low in polycythemia vera but high in secondary polycythemia . Arterial oxygen saturation Laboratory findings (Cont.)

Category A ( major ) Category B ( minor ) Elevated red cell mass ( In men, Hb >18.5 g/ dL or HCT >0.52 and in women, Hb >16.5 g/ dL or HCT >0.48). JAK2-V617F mutation Hypercellular bone marrow Low erythropoietin ( EPO ) EEC growth in vitro Criteria for diagnosis of polycythaemia ( rubra ) vera Diagnosis of PV requires that the patient meets both major criteria plus one minor criterion or the first major criterion and two minor criteria.

PV Treatment Treatment focuses on decreasing the hematocrit to reduce plasma viscosity and its attendant complications. The goal of therapy is a hematocrit <45% and a platelet count < 400,000. Therapeutic options include: Phlebotomy In a newly diagnosed patient, phlebotomy (450mL) should be made two or three times weekly until the haematocrit is in the range of 40-45%, then as necessary to maintain haematocrit within this range Myelosuppressive agents such as Hydroxyurea , radioactive phosphorus and busulfan . Alpha interferon is also an option. - A small daily dose of aspirin is recommended for its anti-platelet effect. - Allopurinol to prevent urate nephropathy

Prognosis Without therapy, median survival of patients with PV is only 6-18 months, but is more than 10 years with treatment. Major causes of death are thrombosis and hemorrhage. Up to 20% of patients develop acute myelogeneous leukemia or myelodysplastic syndrome which are fatal. PV patients can develop a “spent phase” late in their courses that resembles chronic idiopathic myelofibrosis with cytopenia and marrow hypoplasia and fibrosis – referred to as post polycythemic myelofibrosis or secondary myelofibrosis . Post polycythemic myelofibrosis frequently transforms to acute leukemia.

ESSENTIAL THROMBOCYTHEMIA (ET) Clonal myeloproliferative disorder that involves primarily the megakaryocyte cell line. It leads to the dysregulated production of large numbers of mature megakaryocytes in the marrow resulting in marked rise in platelet counts. The etiology of ET is unknown. JAK2 mutation are found in approximately 50% of patients with ET.
ET Epidemiology The incidence of the disease is 2-3/100,000 individuals annually. Usually occurs at the age of 50-60 years. A second peak occurs at approximately 30 years of age, typically in women.

ET Clinical features Many patients are asymptomatic and discovered when a routine blood count is performed. Bleeding manifestation and a predisposition to thrombotic events are the main clinical findings Thrombotic events include strokes, TIA, retinal artery or venous occlusions, coronary artery ischemia, pulmonary embolism, hepatic or portal vein thrombosis, DVT and digital ischemia.

ET Clinical features Erythromelalgia is classic of ET and is believed to be due to microvascular thrombosis of the digital vessel of fingers and toes. Spontaneous abortion due to placental thrombosis. Bleeding occurs most commonly from mucosal surfaces especially the gastrointestinal tract. There may be mild splenomegaly and less often hepatomegaly .

ET Clinical features Transformation of ET to acute myeloid leukemia or a myelodysplastic syndrome occurs in fewer than 5% of patients. There can also be delayed disease transformation into a fibrotic state called post thrombocythemia myeloid metaplasia or myelofibrosis

ET Lab features Peripheral blood film shows marked thrombocytosis . The platelets often display anisocytosis (range from tiny forms to giant platelets). The white blood cell count and differential are usually normal. The red blood cells are normocytic and normochromic. Leukoerythroblastosis . The bone marrow biopsy is usually hypercellular . The most striking abnormality is marked proliferation of large and giant megakaryocytes , usually occurring in loose clusters.

Diagnostic Criteria for ET 1. Persistent elevation of the platelet count ≥450 x 10 9 /L. 2. Megakaryocyte proliferation with large and mature morphology: little or no granulocyte or erythroid proliferation. 3. Not meeting WHO criteria for CML , PV, PMF , MDS, or other myeloid neoplasm. 4. Demonstration of JAK2-V617F or other clonal marker or in the absence of a clonal marker, no evidence of reactive thrombocytosis .

ET Treatment and Prognosis ET is an indolent disorder, characterised by long symptom free intervals, interrupted by occasional life-threatening thromboembolic or hemorrhagic episodes. Most patients enjoy a normal life expectancy. Risk stratification in ET is primarily based upon factors that influence the occurrence of thrombotic complications. Patients are considered to be at high risk if they are > 60 years of age and/or have a prior history of thrombosis.

ET Treatment and Prognosis Therapeutic options include: Low dose Acetyl salicylic acid as an antiplatelet agent (e.g. effective in erythromelalgia ), Hydroxyurea (inhibits platelet production), Anagrelide (inhibits platelet aggregation and has a platelet lowering effect), Alpha Interferon and Radiophosphorous .

parsed.text: CASE BASED STUDY - AML Part 1 - THE OPPOSITION JOURNALIST A 32 year old journalist went to the home of a popular politician to interview him on the upcoming elections. The broadcaster had an opposition leaning and the politician found him to be hostile in his questioning. He criticized each program and policy being put forward by the popular politician and even accused him of fraud. On departure, the broadcaster was given a brown envelope which he opened to find N50,000 in cash and some whitish powdery substance which he paid no attention to. A week later, the journalist presented to the ER complaining of fever, lethargy and mucosal bleeding. The symptoms began 3 days ago, but before then he had been in a general state of good health. He smoked 10-12 sticks of cigarettes daily and had been doing this for 10years. The past medical history was unremarkable. On physical exam, he appeared ill, pale and in moderate acute distress, numerous purpura were found on his upper and lower extremities which the patient said erupted over the past several days. No hepatosplenomegaly or enlarged lymph nodes were noted. CBC and examination of the peripheral blood smear showed mild anaemia (Hb = 9.1g/dl) with numerous schistocytes (red blood cell fragments). Severe thrombocytopenia (10.3 × 10 9 /L) and many circulating atypical mononuclear cells – blasts were also seen (WBC = 44.1 × 10 9 /L). These mononuclear cells made up 36% of circulating nucleated cells in the peripheral blood. Additional laboratory studies showed a markedly prolonged prothrombin time and decreased fibrinogen. Questions: What is your working diagnosis? What are the predisposing factors in the history physical examination and laboratory findings that support your diagnosis? How would you further investigate this patient? What are the lines of management available for this disease? Classify Acute Myeloid Leukaemia What are your differential diagnoses? What does the prolonged prothrombin time & decreased fibrinogen indicate? Part 2 A posterior iliac crest bone marrow aspirate and core biopsy were performed. The bone marrow biopsy and aspirate smear revealed a markedly hypercellular bone marrow with 80% promyelocytes, many with prominent azurophilic granulation and abnormal kidney-bean shaped nuclei. Some of the promyelocytes contained multiple Auer rods (“faggot cells”). Cytochemical staining with myeloperoxidase (MPO) and Sudan-black B showed strong staining in these promyelocytes. Flow cytometric analysis of bone marrow showed a cell population expressing CD13, CD33, CD45(dim), CD117, while lacking HLA-DR. A specimen was also sent for cytogenetic studies. Inter-phase FISH studies showed 95% of cells positive for the PML-RARα fusion, indicative of the t(15:17) translocation. Treatment & Follow up: clinical features and laboratory parameters returned to normal after the first course of treatment. Questions: What is the diagnosis? What role does cytochemical staining have in the diagnosis? What cell line does the flow cytometric analysis above suggest? What type of AML is associated with t(15:17)? What is your diagnosis and classification (FAB & WHO)? What kind of remission did the patient have? What is remission in leukaemia treatment? What is the function of ATRA in AML- M3 treatment? He had dedicated his life and sacrificed his family and relationships for the advancement of the topic. He had no significant past medical history when he was admitted to the emergency room for bruises suffered from a fall from his bike when knocked down by a rough driving “keke Napep”. He however recalled he suffered mild upper abdominal pain, malaise, anorexia, weight loss, and low-grade fever of 1-month’s duration prior to the accident even though he felt this was due to his increase infrequency and duration of bike rides. Platelet count was normal (278,000 × 10 9 cells/L), WBC Differential count result was as follows: Neutrophils: 4.3%, Lymphocytes: 93.8%, Monocytes: 1.3%, Eosinophils: 0.2%, Basophils: 0.4% Peripheral blood and bone marrow aspirate smears were performed. These samples were thereafter sent for immunophenotyping. Questions: What is your working diagnosis and why? Dr Ademola Adewoyin

Objectives

 Categories of haemostasis

secondary haemostasis

Definition
 Haemostasis is the mechanism that
keeps blood in a fluid state
 Normal hemostasis is dependent
upon the complex interaction of
plasma coagulation and fibrinolytic
proteins, platelets, and the blood
vasculature.

-- 3 of 117 --

Normal haemostasis can be div.
into:
The 3 categories are:
 Primary hemostasis: the formation
of the platelet plug.
 Secondary hemostasis: formation of
fibrin through the coagulation
cascade.
 Tertiary hemostasis: the formation
of plasmin for breakdown of the clot.

-- 4 of 117 --

 5 major components are involved in
haemostasis
◼ Blood vessels
◼ Blood platelets
◼ Coagulation factors
◼ Coagulation inhibitors
◼ Fibrinolysis

-- 5 of 117 --

Blood platelets
 Are fragments of cytoplasm of
megakaryocytes
 Non- nucleated
 Produced mainly by the bone marrow
 Normal platelet count- 95-400 x 109/l
 Life span is about 7-10 days
 About 1/3 is trapped in the normal
spleen

-- 6 of 117 --

 Measures about 3x0.5μm
 Volume about 7-11 fl
 Contains 3 types of storage granules
◼ Dense granules
◼ Alpha/specific granules
◼ lysosomes

-- 7 of 117 --

 Specific granules contain:
◼ Fibrinogen
◼ Factor V
◼ vWF
◼ Platelet-derived growth factor
◼ Fibronectin
◼ Β-thromboglobulin
◼ Heparin antagonist(PF-4)
◼ Thrombospodin
◼ Other coagulation factors

-- 8 of 117 --

Dense granules:
 Nucleotides(ADP,ATP,5-HT)
 Calcium
 Serotonin
Lysosomes contain catalase

-- 9 of 117 --

Platelet function
 Main function is the formation of
haemostatic plugs in response to
vascular injury
 Lack of platelet may lead to
spontaneous leakage of blood
through vessel walls

-- 10 of 117 --

Primary haemostasis
 Primary hemostasis is defined as the
formation of the primary platelet plug
and involves platelets, the blood
vessel wall and von Willebrand factor.
 Abnormalities result in hemorrhage
from mucosal surfaces, petechial or
ecchymotic hemorrhages, and
prolonged bleeding after venipuncture
or wounds

-- 11 of 117 --

 The normal endothelium prevents
hemostasis by providing a physical
barrier and by secreting products
which inhibit platelets, including nitric
oxide and prostaglandin I2
(prostacyclin)

-- 12 of 117 --

 The formation of the primary platelet plug involves
platelet adhesion followed by platelet activation then
aggregation to form a platelet plug.
 This function is achieved trough:
❖ Platlet-vessel wall interaction (Adhesion)
❖ Platelet-platelet interaction (Aggregation)
❖ Platelet release reaction

Platelet adhesion
 The 1st event in hemostasis is the adhesion of
platelets to exposed subendothelium.
 In areas of high shear rate (in the
microvasculature), this is mediated vWf, which
binds to gp Ib in the platelet membrane.
 In areas of low shear rate (e.g. aorta),
fibrinogen mediates the binding of platelets to
the gp Ia/IIa).

-- 15 of 117 --

Platelet activation
 The adhesion of platelets to the vessel wall
activates them,
❖ platelets to change shape,
❖ activate the collagen receptor on their surface (an
integrin receptor called glycoprotein IIb/IIIa)
❖ undergo the release reaction (release alpha and
dense granule constituents).
❖ platelets synthesize and release TXA2 and platelet
activating factor (PAF), which are potent platelet
aggregating agonists and vasoconstrictors

-- 16 of 117 --

Platelet aggregation
❖ Platelet aggregation is mediated primarily by fibrinogen
(vWf) has a secondary role), which binds to glycoprotein
IIb/IIIa on adjacent platelets.
❖ This aggregation leads to the formation of the primary
platelet plug, which must be stabilized by the formation
of fibrin.
❖ Platelet procoagulant activity
❖ Following platelet aggregation and release, the exposed
membrane phosplolipid(PF3) is then available for the
tenase and prothrombinase reactions in secondary
haemostasis

-- 17 of 117 --

Blood coagulation(20 haemostasis)
 It’s a biological amplification system xterized by
sequential activation of a cascade of circulating
precursors (coagulation factor enzymes)
culminating in the generation of thrombin
 This involves
❖ circulating coagulation factors, which act as
enzymes [which require activation]
❖ cofactors (factors V and VIII),
❖ calcium and
❖ platelets (platelets provide a source of phospholipid
[PF3] and a binding surface upon which the
coagulation cascade proceeds).

-- 18 of 117 --

Defects in Coagulation
 Defects in the coagulation cascade manifest as
more serious bleeding than primary hemostasis,
including bleeding into cavities (chest, joints) and
subcutaneous hematomas. Petechial hemorrhages
are not seen in disorders of secondary hemostasis.
 These disorders do share common bleeding
symptoms with defects in primary hemostasis,
including epistaxis and bleeding after surgery or
wounds- this may be the 1st sign of a hemostatic
defect, it may be impossible to distinguish between
defects in these 2 pathways based on clinical signs
alone.

Bidirectional incompatible: Both types of incompatibility are present.

--- Slide 46 ---
Platelet RH compatibility Platelets do not express Rh antigens, but platelet components contain residual intact RBCs or fragments that can result in alloimmunization to RBC antigens, including RhD .

Understanding Major and minor ABO incompatiblity The question to ask: Who Has The Antibody that can cause harm If recipient: =Major incompatibility; e.g. Recipient is blood group O implies has anti A and anti B, Donor is blood group A, Implies has anti-B. Recipent who is AB has no antibody that can harm donor cells. But donor donor who is A, B or O has antibody that can harm recipient cell but in relatively lower volume hence is a minor mismatch If both donor and recipient has : Bi-directional

In conclusion Two factors to be considered when issuing platelet concentrates are Compatibility and risk of transfusion Inventory given it’s given the short shelf life

BLOOD TRANSFUSION REACTIONS Dr A. A Ogbenna
--- Slide 2 ---
Transfusion Reactions Transfusion Reactions are adverse reactions associated with the transfusion of blood and its components ANY unfavorable consequence is considered a transfusion reaction of blood TX The risks of transfusion must be weighed against the benefits style.visibility
--- Slide 3 ---
Types of Transfusion Reactions Acute < 24hrs Delayed>24hrs immunologic non immunologic immunologic non immunologic Transfusion reactions Hemolytic Febrile-non hemolytic Allergic Anaphylactic; Transfusion Reaction of Acute Lung injury (TRALI) Hemolytic (Physical or Chemical destruction of RBC) Circulatory overload Air embolus Hypocalcemia Hypothermia Hemolytic Graft vs. Host Disease Posttransfusion Purpura Iron Overload infections
--- Slide 4 ---
ACUTE IMMUNOLOGIC TRANSFUSION REACTIONS Red cell Plasma protein WBC
--- Slide 5 ---
RBC WBC Plasma proteins Allergy Anaphylaxis
--- Slide 6 ---
Acute Haemolytic Transfusion Reaction Etiology: bld grp incompatibility. Antibodies in recipient lead to intravascular destruction of donated RBC. Usually due to ABO incompatibility Occurs within minites Prevention: Give ABO compatible blood. Clinical features: Pain along infusion site Shock Abnormal bleeding/DIC/ Haemoglobinemia/uria Release of cytokines: fever, hypotension Renal failure/ Oliguria, may progress to…anuria Fever, flank pain and reddish brown urine
--- Slide 7 ---
Febrile Non Haemolytic Transfusion Reaction Definition: An INCREASE in temperature of 1 O C during infusion of blood component Usually “mild & benign” = not life threatening Non-haemolytic Etiology : Recipient antibodies to donor WBCs & Cytokines in the transfused blood component. discharge was noted from the cervix. The GC and
Chlamydia cultures were obtained. No blood was
noted. Pelvic bimanual examination revealed
masses up to the umbilicus.

-- 3 of 28 --

ER work-up
 Lab: WBC of 16, HB 3.9, HCT 12.8, PLT
287,000, MCV 64.7, BMP- normal, UA - 1+
Hb and 1+ leukocyte esterase, beta HCG -
291,000.
 Pelvic US: IUP at 10-1/7th weeks and also
complex bilateral adnexal masses with
cysts. Each was approximately 10 x 14 x 7
and 10 x 12 x 8 centimeters.

-- 4 of 28 --

ER Treatment
 Admission
 IV fluids
 Evaluation of her anemia
 Transfusion with 2 units of blood
 Evaluation of bilateral adnexal masses: CA-
125. Consider further imaging.

-- 5 of 28 --

Issues
 Blood Bank issues: B negative, anti-D (1:256)
and anti-C(1:1) present, concerned with HDN,
currently 10+ weeks pregnancy, not a
candidate for RhoGam
 Anemia: iron deficient, started on iron
supplement, no source of bleeding found,
smear – 2+ spherocytes, 3+ microcytes, 2+
fragmented cells, HB studies – 98% Hb A, 1.2%
Hb A2, 0.5%Hb F, no Hb S, C

-- 6 of 28 --

Issues
 Adneal masses: CT - no lymphadenopathy, no
metastasis, cystic mass with no papillary
projections or solid part, c/w overstimulation
syndrome. TSH high (41.7), T4 <1mcg/dl, T3 23
ng/dl, both low
 Cardiovascular. a right sided DVT, starting
heparin, possibly secondary to venous stasis
from her adnexal masses. Base PTT 25, PT

rheumatology studies ordered

-- 7 of 28 --

Hemolytic Disease of Newborn
 Definition: a hemolytic disease in the newborn
caused by blood-type incompatibility between
mother and child
 Maternal Ig G antibodies can cross the placenta
and coating fetal RBCs – hemolysis
 Maternal sensitization: history of transfusion or
pregnancy

-- 8 of 28 --



-- 9 of 28 --



-- 10 of 28 --

Common RBC antigens causing
HDN
--Rh antigens. Most common is D antigen, next is c
antigen. IgG can cross placenta.
– ABO antigens: only in infants born to group O
mothers because some have IgG anti-A, anti-B,
anti-A,B antibodies without sensitization, usually
mild HDN
– Kell: Kell antigens are expressed in early fetal
RBCs and bone marrow hematopoietic cells –
cause hemolysis and bone marrow suppression –
severe and early HDN
– Kidd, MNSs, Duffy antigens: rare, but increasing

-- 11 of 28 --

Prevention of HDN
 Nearly all women with Rh negative or weak D
type are identified in early pregnancy by blood
testing.
 If mother is Rh-, anti-D is negative,usually given
Rh immunoglobulin (RhIg), also known as
RhoGAM
– 1 vial (300 mcg), around the 28th week of
pregnancy
– at time when vaginal bleeding occurs (calculate)
– at the time of delivery within 72 hours

-- 12 of 28 --

Maternal-Fetal Bleeding Screening
 After vaginal bleeding or delivery, if
screening is negative, just give 1 vial (300
mcg) RhIG. If +, give minimal 2 vials and
add more vials after calculation

-- 13 of 28 --

Calculating Dosage of RhoGam
First perform the Kleihauer-
Betke test to get the
percentage of fetal red
cells in the mother
 Mechanism
 Blood smear stained with
acid elution
 Hb F is more acid resistant
 Fetal RBC darkly stained,
Maternal RBC "ghosts"
Fetal Blood
Maternal Blood

-- 14 of 28 --

Calculating Dosage of RhoGam
Hemoglobin electrophoresis on
cellulose acetate Hemoglobin HPLC

-- 15 of 28 --

Calculating Dosage of RhoGam
Method 1:
% of fetal RBC X 50 / 30
Method 2:
If the decimal <0.5,
round up; if the decimal
is >0.5, round up and
then round up again

-- 16 of 28 --

First Sensitized Pregnancy
 Father RBC phenotyping:
– negative for the offending antigen then no further
testing is necessary
– positive for the antigen, serial antibody titer
monitoring is required
 Anti-K: HDN tends to happen early and severe
– Frequency of monitoring: every 4 weeks to 28
weeks, then every 2 weeks until birth
– Critical titer: 1:8 or above

-- 17 of 28 --

First Sensitized Pregnancy
 Non anti-K antibodies
– Frequency of monitoring: first at 12 weeks gestation,
then at 28, 32 weeks gestation
– Critical titer : the IAT titer is > 1:32 or albumin titer >
1:16 (it varies from hospital to hospital)
– IAT titers of < 1:32 or less are managed non-invasively
with repeat antibody titers every 2-4 weeks.
– IAT > 32: Doppler Ultrasound to measure peak
systolic velocity of middle cerebral artery or
amniocentesis or umbilical blood sampling q 2 to 3
weeks to detect fetal anemia . (N Engl J Med. 2000 Jan
6;342(1):9-14 )

-- 18 of 28 --

the median hemoglobin concentration). Triangles indicate fetuses with moderate or

circles indicate the fetuses with hydrops. The solid curve indicates the median peak
systolic velocity in the middle cerebral artery, and the dotted curve indicates 1.5

-- 19 of 28 --

Amniocentesis
 Bilirubin level: measured by
spectrophotometrically measuring absorbance at
the 450-nm wavelength in a specimen of amniotic
fluid that has been shielded from light ---- Liley
curve
 Fetal genotyping
– For RhE, Rhe, RhC, Rhc, Kell ,and Cellano (k) the
parents' DNA should be tested concurrently
 Cytogenetic testing to screen for congenital
disease

-- 20 of 28 --

The Liley Curve
Amniotic fluid bilirubin level (log), vs weeks of pregancy
Zone 1: low risk
Zone 2: intermediate
risk
Zone 3: high risk

-- 21 of 28 --

Umbilical Cord Blood Sampling
 Direct measurement of fetal blood bilirubin
and hemoglobin level
 Fetal RBC phenotyping
 Technique can be used for fetal blood
transfusion or exchange
 More complications

-- 22 of 28 --

Hemoglobin Concentrations in 265 Normal Fetuses and 111 Fetuses That
Underwent Cordocentesis

-- 23 of 28 --

Previously Affected Pregnancy
 For patients with a previously affected
pregnancy, the timing of the initial procedure
(serial amniocentesis) is determined by past
clinical history. It is usually performed at
least 4-8 weeks earlier than the prior
gestational age at which significant
morbidity occurred.

-- 24 of 28 --

 In women with extremely high titers ( > 256), at
less than 28 weeks, where the fetus does not
demonstrate hydrops, and there is a documented
history of fetal death due to hydrops ---- IVIG
might be offered. The dose is 400 mg/kg per day
for 5 days, with repeat infusions every 15 to 21
days. Specific contraindications to intravenous
immunoglobulin use include a previous episode of
IVIG-induced anaphylaxis (rare) and selective IgA
deficiency.

-- 25 of 28 --

Symptoms of HDN
 During pregnancy:
 Mild anemia, hyperbilirubinemia, and jaundice
 Severe anemia with enlargement of the liver and
spleen
 Hydrops fetalis - The heart begins to fail due to severe
anemia and large amounts of fluid build up in the
tissues and organs, at great risk of being stillborn.
 After birth:
 Severe hyperbilirubinemia and jaundice
 Kernicterus - the most severe form of
hyperbilirubinemia and results from the buildup of
bilirubin in the brain. This can cause seizures, brain
damage, deafness and death.

-- 26 of 28 --

Diagnosis
 Mother’s blood: RBC antibodies
 Doppler Ultrasound - to detect organ enlargement
or fluid buildup in the fetus.
 Amniocentesis - to measure the amount of
bilirubin in the amniotic fluid.
 Fetal umbilical cord blood: antibodies, bilirubin,
and anemia
 Newborn: umbilical cord blood for blood group,
red blood cell count and antibodies, newborn
peripheral blood testing for bilirubin levels.

-- 27 of 28 --

Treatment
 During pregnancy:
– Intrauterine blood transfusion of red blood cells, into the
abdominal cavity of the fetus or directly into the umbilical
cord vein
– Early delivery if the fetus develops complications -prevent
worsening of HDN.
 After birth:
– Blood transfusions (for severe anemia).
– Phototherapy
– Intravenous fluids (for low blood pressure).
– Help for respiratory distress using oxygen or a mechanical
ventilation
– Exchange transfusion

What other serious reactions should be considered in the differential diagnosis at this point? Management: What are the immediate steps you should take as the clinician? Pathophysiology: Briefly explain the proposed mechanism for this reaction. Prevention: What interventions could be used to prevent this reaction in the future for this patient? Case 2: The Surgical Emergency Patient: A 45-year-old female with a history of uterine fibroids is undergoing an elective hysterectomy. She has no known history of transfusions. During surgery, she experiences significant blood loss and is transfused with 2 units of PRBCs rapidly, under pressure. Event: As the second unit is being infused, the patient's blood pressure drops from 110/70 mmHg to 70/40 mmHg. Her heart rate increases from 85 bpm to 120 bpm. The anesthesiologist notes that the surgical field is becoming increasingly "oozey" and there is abnormal bleeding from the IV site. The patient is oliguric and has developed reddish-brown urine. She is febrile to 39.0°C. The patient is under anesthesia and cannot report symptoms like pain or dyspnea. Questions: Diagnosis: What is the most likely diagnosis? Why is this considered a "life-threatening" emergency? Clinical Features: Based on the scenario, identify the key clinical features that support this diagnosis. Investigations: What investigations should be performed immediately to confirm the diagnosis and assess the severity of the reaction? (Consider lab tests, blood products, and clerical checks). Management: What is the immediate management plan for this patient? Case 3: The Complex Patient with Respiratory Distress Patient: A 65-year-old female with a history of congestive heart failure and chronic anemia is admitted for a worsening cough and fatigue. She is given a transfusion of 1 unit of PRBCs. Event: About 2 hours into the transfusion, she develops sudden and severe shortness of breath. On examination, she is tachypneic (30/min), tachycardic (115 bpm), and hypertensive (160/95 mmHg). Auscultation of the lungs reveals crackles throughout both lung fields. An oxygen saturation monitor shows 88% on room air. A chest X-ray is ordered and shows pulmonary edema with an enlarged cardiac silhouette. Questions: Diagnosis: What is the most likely diagnosis? What key feature helps differentiate this from another important respiratory reaction (TRALI)? Risk Factors: What risk factors does this patient have that predispose her to this condition? Pathophysiology: Explain the mechanism behind this reaction. Management: What is the immediate and subsequent management for this patient? Case 4: The Immunocompromised Host Patient: A 22-year-old male who underwent a bone marrow transplant for leukemia 3 months ago is admitted for anemia. He is currently on immunosuppressive therapy to prevent graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). He is transfused with 2 units of non-irradiated PRBCs from his sister (a haploidentical match). Event: Seven days after the transfusion, he develops a fever, a maculopapular rash that progresses to blistering (bullae), and watery diarrhea. He also complains of nausea and abdominal cramps. Lab work shows new pancytopenia (low WBC, RBC, and platelets) and elevated liver function tests and bilirubin. Questions: Diagnosis: What is the most likely diagnosis? Epidemiology & Pathophysiology: Why is this patient at high risk for this reaction? What is the underlying mechanism? Prevention: How could this reaction have been prevented? Treatment: What are the general principles of managing this patient now? Case 5. A 32-year-old woman is receiving a unit of packed red blood cells for symptomatic anaemia. About 20 minutes after commencement of the transfusion, she develops chills, fever, back pain and shortness of breath. The nurse stops the transfusion and calls you to review the patient. As the House-officer, describe the steps you would take in the assessment and immediate management of this patient.

Isoagglutinin (naturally occurring ABO antibodies) Isoagglutinins are naturally occurring antibodies directed against the ABO blood group antigens that are absent on an individual's own red blood cells . Origin: Develop during the first 3–6 months of life following exposure to environmental antigens (e.g., gut bacteria and dietary substances) that resemble ABO antigens. Optimal reaction temperature: React best at room temperature (20–24°C) and are highly active at 37°C in incompatible transfusions. Clinical significance: Cause ABO-incompatible transfusion reactions , which are often severe and characterized by acute intravascular haemolysis . CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE OF RED CELL ANTIBODY Introduction The discovery of red cell antigens and antibodies forms the scientific basis of immunohaematology , also known as blood banking or transfusion medicine . Laboratory investigations involving red cell antigen-antibody reactions are routinely performed to: Determine an individual's blood group. Select compatible blood for transfusion. Prevent haemolytic transfusion reactions. Detect maternal antibodies that may cause haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN). Diagnose autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA). Investigate unexpected transfusion reactions. These investigations rely on the principle that an antibody binds specifically to its corresponding antigen , producing visible agglutination or haemolysis.
--- Slide 37 ---
1. ABO Blood Grouping Definition ABO blood grouping is the laboratory determination of the ABO blood group by identifying: Antigens present on red blood cells. Naturally occurring antibodies present in plasma. Since ABO incompatibility may cause fatal acute haemolytic transfusion reactions, ABO grouping is the first and most important pre-transfusion test
--- Slide 38 ---
ABO Blood grouping Cont’d Principle The patient's red cells are mixed with commercially prepared antisera. If the corresponding antigen is present, agglutination occurs. Example Anti-A + A cells → Agglutination Anti-B + B cells → Agglutination No antigen → No agglutination

--- Slide 40 ---
Methods of Blood grouping Cont’d B. Reverse (Serum) Grouping Tests plasma antibodies. Patient serum is tested against: Known A cells Known B cells Example
--- Slide 41 ---

--- Slide 42 ---

--- Slide 43 ---

--- Slide 44 ---
Principle Patient serum is incubated with commercially prepared screening red cells that possess many clinically important antigens. Agglutination indicates that an unexpected antibody is present. Clinical Uses Performed: Before blood transfusion During pregnancy Before organ transplantation
--- Slide 45 ---
