Each panel cell possesses a known antigen profile. By observing the reaction pattern, the specific antibody is identified. Example Positive reactions only with cells possessing the Kell antigen suggest: Anti-K antibody. Importance Allows the blood bank to supply: Antigen-negative compatible blood.
--- Slide 46 ---
Crossmatching Definition Crossmatching is the final compatibility test performed before blood transfusion. It confirms that donor blood is compatible with the recipient.
--- Slide 47 ---
TYPES OF BLOOD CROSSMATCH Types Major Crossmatch Recipient serum + Donor red cells (at Rm temp, at 37 0c , with albumin, with Antihumanglobulin -AHG) This is the most important test. Minor Crossmatch Donor serum Recipient red cells Rarely performed today.
--- Slide 48 ---
CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE OF RED CELL ANTIBODY 1. Haemolytic transfusion reaction: Intravascular Immediate transfusion reaction: ABO Delayed: KIDD ( Jk a , JK b )
--- Slide 49 ---
Extravascular : IgG1 and IgG3 reacting at body temperature( IgG antibodies of Rh , Kidd, Kell , Duffy or Ss antigen) and these make up the bulk of clinically significant antibodies
--- Slide 50 ---
Auto immune Haemolytic anaemia : arising from viral infection, drugs leading to break down in immune system tolerance to self antigen, or from exposure to foreign antigen that induce antibodies that cross-react with self red cell antigen.
--- Slide 51 ---
Most cold reactive auto-antibodies have anti-I activity. In paroxysymal cold haemoglobinuria ( Donarth - landsteiner -antibody- a biphasic haemolysin an igG seen in children after a viral illness or vacination ) reaction with P-antigen cause attachment to red cell in the cold and efficiently activates complement before it dissociates at warmer temp.
--- Slide 52 ---

--- Slide 53 ---
Haemolytic Disease of the newborn a.k.a erythroblastosis fetalis IgG1 and IgG3 which crosses placenta are mostly implicated
--- Slide 54 ---
HDN cont,d Aetio -pathogenesis 1. Rhesus related 2. ABO related 3. other red cell antigen/antibody
--- Slide 55 ---
Rhesus related 1. sensitization of rhesus negative mothers: previous blood transfusion using Rh + donors, fetal transfusion: abortions of Rh positive fetus, abruption placenta etc 2. more severe phenotype: because Rh antigens are more concentrated on red cells, fully developed in-utero 3. critical titer is 1:32: fetal hydrops
--- Slide 56 ---
ABO related 1. affects women with blood group O+ with a high titer of immune anti A or B. and a fetus with blood group A or B. women 2. it is usually less severe: ABH antigen is widely distributed on virtually all nucleated cells; ABO is not fully developed till after birth
--- Slide 57 ---
Other red cell antigen/antibodies Over 50 other red cell surface antigens have been implicated in HDN ( E.g Kell , duffy - - Fya ). However only anti- Rhc and anti- kell (K1) are associated with severe disease. Critical value for k1 is 1:8
--- Slide 58 ---
Clinical features Pale skin Yellowish amniotic fluid, umbilical cord and eyes Enlarged liver and or spleen. Hydrops fetalis ( massive edema, heart failure and organomegally ) kernicterus
--- Slide 59 ---
Laboratory features Anaemia Thrombocytopaenia Peripheral blood film: erythro-leucoblastic features polychromasia
--- Slide 60 ---
diagnosis Amniocentesis Percutaneous umbilical cord blood sampling ultrasonography

treatment Prophylaxis (maternal after a Keilhauer test) Intra-uterine transfusion Early delivery Phototherapy Exchange blood transfusion Intravenous immunoglobulin

These investigations rely on the principle that an antibody binds specifically to its corresponding antigen , producing visible agglutination or haemolysis.

1. ABO Blood Grouping Definition ABO blood grouping is the laboratory determination of the ABO blood group by identifying: Antigens present on red blood cells. Naturally occurring antibodies present in plasma. Since ABO incompatibility may cause fatal acute haemolytic transfusion reactions, ABO grouping is the first and most important pre-transfusion test

ABO Blood grouping Cont’d Principle The patient's red cells are mixed with commercially prepared antisera. If the corresponding antigen is present, agglutination occurs. Example Anti-A + A cells → Agglutination Anti-B + B cells → Agglutination No antigen → No agglutination

METHODS OF BLOOD GROUPING {5C22544A-7EE6-4342-B048-85BDC9FD1C3A} Blood Group (RECIPIENT RED CELLS) Anti-A Anti-B A + − B − + AB + + O − − A. Forward (Cell) Grouping Tests red cell antigens. Patient's red cells are reacted with: Anti-A Anti-B Sometimes Anti-AB Example
Methods of Blood grouping Cont’d B. Reverse (Serum) Grouping Tests plasma antibodies. Patient serum is tested against: Known A cells Known B cells Example
Example of reverse grouping {5C22544A-7EE6-4342-B048-85BDC9FD1C3A} Blood Group (RECIPIENT SERUM) A Cells B Cells A − + B + − AB − − O + +
Why Both Tests Are Performed Forward grouping detects antigens. Reverse grouping confirms antibody pattern. Both results must agree before a blood group is accepted. This is called ABO confirmation

Other red cell antigens with clinical importance in serology Not all antibodies are Anti-A or Anti-B. Patients previously transfused or pregnant may develop antibodies against: Kell Kidd Duffy Rh antigens MNS These antibodies can destroy donor red cells.

Principle Patient serum is incubated with commercially prepared screening red cells that possess many clinically important antigens. Agglutination indicates that an unexpected antibody is present. Clinical Uses Performed: Before blood transfusion During pregnancy Before organ transplantation

Antibody Identification If antibody screening is positive ( coombs test) , the next step is antibody identification. Principle Patient serum is tested against a panel of reagent red cells. Each panel cell possesses a known antigen profile. By observing the reaction pattern, the specific antibody is identified. Example Positive reactions only with cells possessing the Kell antigen suggest: Anti-K antibody. Importance Allows the blood bank to supply: Antigen-negative compatible blood.
Crossmatching Definition Crossmatching is the final compatibility test performed before blood transfusion. It confirms that donor blood is compatible with the recipient.

TYPES OF BLOOD CROSSMATCH Types Major Crossmatch Recipient serum + Donor red cells (at Rm temp, at 37 0c , with albumin, with Antihumanglobulin -AHG) This is the most important test. Minor Crossmatch Donor serum Recipient red cells Rarely performed today.
CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE OF RED CELL ANTIBODY 1. Haemolytic transfusion reaction: Intravascular Immediate transfusion reaction: ABO Delayed: KIDD ( Jk a , JK b )
Extravascular : IgG1 and IgG3 reacting at body temperature( IgG antibodies of Rh , Kidd, Kell , Duffy or Ss antigen) and these make up the bulk of clinically significant antibodies

Auto immune Haemolytic anaemia : arising from viral infection, drugs leading to break down in immune system tolerance to self antigen, or from exposure to foreign antigen that induce antibodies that cross-react with self red cell antigen.

Most cold reactive auto-antibodies have anti-I activity. In paroxysymal cold haemoglobinuria ( Donarth - landsteiner -antibody- a biphasic haemolysin an igG seen in children after a viral illness or vacination ) reaction with P-antigen cause attachment to red cell in the cold and efficiently activates complement before it dissociates at warmer temp.

Feature Agglutination Haemolysis Definition Clumping of red cells Destruction of red cells Caused by Antibody cross-linking RBCs Antibody with or without complement activation Main antibody IgM IgM (intravascular) or IgG (extravascular) Complement required No Usually yes for intravascular haemolysis Main site In vitro or circulation Blood vessels or reticuloendothelial system Clinical outcome Positive blood grouping/crossmatch Transfusion reaction, anaemia, jaundice Comparing hemagglutinins and hemolysins Summary Table
Haemolytic Disease of the newborn a.k.a erythroblastosis fetalis IgG1 and IgG3 which crosses placenta are mostly implicated
HDN cont,d Aetio -pathogenesis 1. Rhesus related 2. ABO related 3. other red cell antigen/antibody

Rhesus related 1. sensitization of rhesus negative mothers: previous blood transfusion using Rh + donors, fetal transfusion: abortions of Rh positive fetus, abruption placenta etc 2. more severe phenotype: because Rh antigens are more concentrated on red cells, fully developed in-utero 3. critical titer is 1:32: fetal hydrops

ABO related 1. affects women with blood group O+ with a high titer of immune anti A or B. and a fetus with blood group A or B. women 2. it is usually less severe: ABH antigen is widely distributed on virtually all nucleated cells; ABO is not fully developed till after birth

Other red cell antigen/antibodies Over 50 other red cell surface antigens have been implicated in HDN ( E.g Kell , duffy - - Fya ). However only anti- Rhc and anti- kell (K1) are associated with severe disease. Critical value for k1 is 1:8
Clinical features Pale skin Yellowish amniotic fluid, umbilical cord and eyes Enlarged liver and or spleen. Hydrops fetalis ( massive edema, heart failure and organomegally ) kernicterus
Laboratory features Anaemia Thrombocytopaenia Peripheral blood film: erythro-leucoblastic features polychromasia
diagnosis Amniocentesis Percutaneous umbilical cord blood sampling ultrasonography
treatment Prophylaxis (maternal after a Keilhauer test) Intra-uterine transfusion Early delivery Phototherapy Exchange blood transfusion Intravenous immunoglobulin

--- Slide 1 ---
The immune system: splenic function and disorders of the spleen THE SPLEEN Prof. OSUNKALU V.O- MB.CH.B, MWACPath , FMCPath, MSc(pub hlth ), MSc( CBG), Ph.D.(genetics)
--- Slide 2 ---
Anatomy of the spleen A specialized connective tissue composed of a 3 dimensional reticular meshwork serving as filter in d path of blood circulation Selectively clears blood of cells, micro organisms and antigens in stroma meshes called filtration beds
--- Slide 3 ---
Splenic Boundaries (Surface Anatomy) The spleen is an intraperitoneal lymphoid organ located in the left upper quadrant (left hypochondrium) The spleen is normally not palpable and is bounded approximately by: Superior: Left hemidiaphragm (separating it from the pleura and left lung) Inferior: Left colic (splenic) flexure
--- Slide 4 ---
Splenic Boundaries (Surface Anatomy) Anterio - medial: Fundus of the stomach Posterio - medial: Left kidney Lateral: Left lower ribs (9th–11th ribs) and diaphragm Clinical relevance: During splenomegaly, the spleen enlarges inferomedially toward the right iliac fossa , becoming palpable below the left costal margin.
--- Slide 5 ---
Types of spleen Sinusal spleen: a.k.a defence spleen seen in cats and humans and accounts for less than 0.25% of body weight. The immunologically active white pulps are particularly prominent where lymphocytes, macrophages and APCs predominate. Non- sinusal or storage spleen are seen in herbivores. Capsules and trabeculae are fibromuscular . Usually heavy with stored blood and thus perform internal transfusion. May make up 1% of body weight
--- Slide 6 ---
Spleen receives 1 to 10% of cardiac output or about 300mils/min in humans Weighs an average of 135g in humans and only only 80g when totally drained of blood. Involution occurs with age- weighs about 70g in elderly
--- Slide 7 ---
Splenic structure The capsule is fibromuscular, covered on the external surface by ciliated cuboidal mesothelium(contributing to its high splenic haematocrit by pumping fluid out) On the medial surface is a ridge called the hilus through which blood vessels traverse the spleen Richly branched trabeculae project into the splenic pulp carrying splenic artery and vein and efferrent lymphatics while dividing the pulp into compartments
--- Slide 9 ---
The nerve supply accompanies the arterial branches, terminating deep in the pulp as adrenergic axons that cause the pulp meshwork to expand and contract. The primary cellular element of the pulp is the branched fibroblastic reticular cells which produces slender collagen fibers(reticular fibers) These fibres (type 4 collagens) together with the reticular cells form the meshwork of the pulp
--- Slide 10 ---
Called the reticulum which is what filters blood(filtration bed)
--- Slide 11 ---
Structure of the filtration bed There are two main distinguishable areas of the filtration bed 1. white pulp 2. red pulp
--- Slide 12 ---
White pulp:from the hilus , the trabeculae traverses the stroma carrying with it a branch of the splenic artery (central artery) As the central artery enters the meshwork of the spleen, its immediately surrounded by distinct layer of reticulum called the periarterial lymphatic sheath. Which itself is encapsuled by the circumferential reticulum This sheath is rich in T-lymphocytes
--- Slide 13 ---
Along the length of the PALS are small round follicles scattered on its peripheral surface. These are ovoid accumulation of B lymphocytes which appears whitish dots on the cut surface of the spleen( malphigian corpuscles) The follicle is made up of central germinal and outer marginal zones As the central artery branches, it diminish in size as it goes, so likewise is the PALS
--- Slide 14 ---
Function of the white pulps Majorly clears and concentrate lymphocytes and accessory cells from circulation Lymphocytes that traffic to and fro the white pulp are the circulating pool On activation the lymphocytes may remain in the spleen to sustain primary or secondary immune response Lymphoid nodules become enlarged as they recruit more B-lymphocytes from the blood and mantle zone and moves in wards forming the germinal center
--- Slide 15 ---
The central arterioles now terminate in the marginal zone as it enters the RED pulp The PALS and lymphoid nodules thus constitutes the white pulp
--- Slide 16 ---
B and T cells have few hours to interact as B cells on their way to the germinal center traverse the PALS B and T lymphocytes exit the spleen via the efferent lymphatics
--- Slide 17 ---
Red pulp Consists of the meshwork called splenic cord of Bilroth along with splenic sinuses Arterial vessels that runs from the center of the PALS supply the marginal zone and red pulp These vessels terminate as arterial capillaries and vessels with trumpet-like flares with widened endothelial slits or pores as the blood runs through numerous interwoven filtration beds
--- Slide 18 ---
Functions of the spleen Immune function: tuftin , prim and secondary Large fraction of circulating neutrophils pool are marginated in the spleen. Slow transit of blood in the red pulp allows close contact of macrophage with antibody and complement coated cells and microorganisms and senescent cells entrapped Non immune function: a third of platelets are stored in the spleen, pooling, pitting
--- Slide 19 ---
hypersplenism In 1899, Chauffard proposed that increased splenic activity results in haemolysis This served as the basis for the first ever splenectomy in 1910 by Suthaland and Burghard in a patient with hereditary spherocytosis
--- Slide 20 ---
The normal and abnormal function of the spleen is traceable to its two major functions: Filtration and immune surveillance of blood in the red pulp and antibody synthesis in the white pulp.
--- Slide 21 ---
Hypersplenism occurs when these functions are 1. appropriately increased as in HS, or ITP or 2. inappropriately increased as in portal hypertension As enunciated by Darmalek : hyperplenism is usually associated with splenomegally , causes cytopaenias,with compensatory BM hyperplasia and is corrected by splenectomy
--- Slide 22 ---
pathogenesis Ideally spleen serves to filter senescent red cells by passing 10% of blood flow through the non endothelialized mesh of the red pulp studded with macophages . The blood then reenters the circulation via narrow slits measuring 1-3 um, in the endothelium of the venous sinuses.
--- Slide 23 ---
With red cell membrane defects or immune disorders, spleen may become over worked with consequent hypertrophy and then sequester normal cells for destruction. Splenomegally due to variety of causes usually increases the proportion of blood channeled through the red pulp causing inappropriate hypersplenic sequestration of both normal abnormal cells- cytopaenia results
--- Slide 24 ---
Bone marrow responds to compensate for the peripheral cytopaenia - BM hyperplasia
--- Slide 25 ---
Causes of splenomegally Idiopathic: TSS Hereditary disorders:Hereditary Spherocytosis, acanthosis, stomatocytosis , thalassaemias Connective tisssue disorders:SLE , Metabolic disorders: amyloidosis, glycogen storage disease, neimann picks, gauchers Malignancies: cml,myelofibrosis , hairy cell leukamias,cll Infections: viral, fungal, parasitic( leishmaniasis
--- Slide 26 ---
Cardio-vascular: CHF, budd-chiari (obstruction of the splenic/portal vein blood flow- clott ), liver chirrosis
--- Slide 27 ---
Tropical splenomegaly syndrome (TSS) Aka hyperactive malarial splenomegaly Follows immunological over-stimulation due to repeated malarial infection over a long period of time Seen in malaria endemic areas(Africa, india ) Its characterized by :
--- Slide 28 ---
1. massive spleen enlargement 2. hepatomegaly 3. marked elevation in serum IgM level 4. elevated antimalarial antibodies 5. markedly dilated sinusoids 6. marked erythrophagocytosis and lymphocyte infiltration of the pulp 7. blood smear for malaria parasite is usually negative
--- Slide 29 ---
Clinical features may include: Anaemia Thrombocytopaenia Management: 1. exclude all other causes of splenomegaly 2.Antimalaria drug followed by prolonged antimalarial prophylaxis

parsed.text: Case 1: ABO-Related Haemolytic Disease of the Newborn "The Unexpected Jaundice in a Term Infant" Clinical Presentation A 38-week gestation male infant is born via spontaneous vaginal delivery. Birth weight is 3.2 kg. Apgar scores are 9 and 9. The mother is Blood Group O, RhD Positive. The father is Blood Group A, RhD Negative. At 14 hours of life, the infant develops progressive jaundice (icterus) affecting the face and upper chest. He is feeding poorly but is haemodynamically stable (normal heart rate, blood pressure, no hepatosplenomegaly). Initial Investigations (at 14 hours) · Neonatal Blood Group: A, RhD Positive. · Direct Antiglobulin Test (DAT): Weakly positive (1+). · Serum Bilirubin: Total 220 µmol/L (12.8 mg/dL) – above phototherapy threshold for his risk factors. · Haemoglobin (Hb): 16.5 g/dL (within normal range for cord blood). · Peripheral Blood Film: Shows numerous spherocytes and polychromasia. Reticulocyte count is elevated (8%). Discussion Questions (Small Group) Pathophysiology: Why is this infant jaundiced despite the mother and baby both being RhD Positive? What specific antibody is likely responsible, and why is it clinically significant that the mother is Group O rather than Group A or B? Diagnostic Dilemma: The DAT is only weakly positive. Why is this so? Differential: What features on the blood film and labs help differentiate this from G6PD deficiency or physiological jaundice? Management: what will be your approach to the management of This baby? Case 2: Clinical Presentation A 32-year-old woman, Gravida 3 Para 2, presents for a routine 34-week obstetric ultrasound. Her booking blood group was A, RhD Negative. Antibody screen at 12 weeks was negative. Her previous two pregnancies were uneventful, and she did not receive Anti-D prophylaxis after her second delivery due to a clerical error. The ultrasound reveals fetal ascites, scalp oedema (skin thickening >5 mm), bilateral pleural effusions, and polyhydramnios. Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA) Doppler shows a peak systolic velocity (PSV) of 1.8 MoM (indicative of severe fetal anaemia). She undergoes an emergency Caesarean section at 34 weeks. Cord Blood Investigations at Birth · Neonatal Blood Group: A, RhD Positive. · DAT: Strongly positive (4+). · Haemoglobin (Hb): 6.8 g/dL (severe anaemia). · Total Bilirubin (Cord): 85 µmol/L (5 mg/dL) – already high at birth. · Reticulocyte Count: Inappropriately low for the degree of anaemia (< 1%). · Peripheral Blood Film: Numerous nucleated RBCs (erythroblasts), anisopoikilocytosis, but few spherocytes. Maternal Investigations (Retrospectively) · Indirect Antiglobulin Test (IAT): Positive. Anti-D antibody titre > 1:256. Discussion Questions Pathophysiology (basic level): Why is the anaemia so much more severe here compared to Case 1 (ABO HDN)? Specifically, explain the mechanism of extramedullary haematopoiesis (hepatosplenomegaly) and why the reticulocyte count is low (erythropoietic suppression) despite profound anaemia. The "Failed Prophylaxis": The mother’s antibody screen was negative at 12 weeks. How did she become sensitised? Why is the disease so severe in this third pregnancy but not necessarily the second? Pathophysiology of Hydrops Fetalis (300L): The fetus has ascites, scalp oedema, and pleural effusions – a picture of hydrops fetalis. Trace the pathophysiological cascade from massive haemolysis to these clinical findings. Why does the liver become enlarged, and how does that worsen the fetal condition? Basic Postnatal Management: What are the immediate management priorities after birth? Explain the mechanism of action of phototherapy – how does it lower bilirubin? Prevention and Long-Term Sequelae (300L): What is kernicterus, and which parts of the central nervous system are primarily affected? More importantly, how could this severe disease have been prevented in this mother’s current and future pregnancies? Describe the rationale.

Which blood component is rich in clotting factors and is used to treat bleeding disorders? a) Platelets b) Fresh Frozen Plasma c) Red Blood Cells d) Granulocyte concentrates 2. What is the primary function of cryoprecipitate in blood component therapy? a) To provide oxygen-carrying capacity b) To enhance clotting capabilities c) To restore plasma volume d) To boost immune response 4. Which blood component therapy is best used to treat bleeding caused by deficiencies in factors VIII and IX? a) Platelet Transfusion b) Whole Blood Transfusion c) Fresh Frozen Plasma Transfusion d) Cryoprecipitate Transfusion 13. Which blood component therapy is used to treat coagulation factor deficiencies in patients with liver disease? a) Platelet Transfusion b) Whole Blood Transfusion c) Fresh Frozen Plasma Transfusion d) Granulocyte transfusion 16. A patient receiving a blood transfusion develops chills, fever, and headache. Which type of blood transfusion reaction can cause acute kidney injury (AKI) due to intravascular haemolysis? a) Allergic reaction b) Haemolytic reaction c) Febrile non-haemolytic reaction d) Anaphylactic reaction 9. What is the primary cause of anaphylactic transfusion reactions? a) Mismatched blood types b) Bacterial contamination c) Allergic response to plasma proteins d) Haemolytic reaction 12.
